distractor_explanations.How the sequence of events determines th: Confusing point of view with plot sequence, so that who reports the events is mistaken for the order in which they happen Both versions recount the same events in the same order, so plot is held constant while perspective changes. This option reflects the common misconception that point of view concerns the order of happenings. Plot is what happens; point of view is who reports it.

subject: Teaching Reading
stem: A fourth-grade class reads a short play. The teacher asks students to note what characters say to one another, what the stage directions tell the actors to do, and where the scenes break. This work primarily helps students understand
choices: How a character's decisions drive the events of the plot
How to write a summary that includes only the most important events
How the structural features of drama, including dialogue, stage directions, and scenes, carry meaning that prose paragraphs do not
How the rhyme and rhythm of a poem contribute to its mood
correct_answer: How the structural features of drama, including dialogue, stage directions, and scenes, carry meaning that prose paragraphs do not
explanation: The question requires an understanding of how the structural elements of different genres contribute to a text's overall meaning. In drama, meaning lives in what is spoken, in the directions that convey action and tone, and in the division of scenes that signals shifts in time or place, so reading those features is what allows students to interpret the play at all.

distractor_explanations.How a character's decisions drive the ev: Confusing structural features of a text with elements of story content, so character motivation is studied in place of genre form Following what characters decide is interpretation of content, not attention to the structural elements named in the activity. This option reflects the common misconception that any discussion of a literary text counts as structural analysis. The teacher pointed students at dialogue, directions, and scene breaks, which are formal features.
distractor_explanations.How to write a summary that includes onl: Reducing drama to a summary of main events, which discards the stage directions and scene breaks that carry meaning Summarizing reduces a text to its gist and leaves out the very details this activity asks students to notice. This option reflects the common misconception that the purpose of reading any text is to extract the main events. In drama, stage directions and scene breaks are essential and are lost in a summary.
distractor_explanations.How the rhyme and rhythm of a poem contr: Applying the sound features of poetry to a play, so that rhyme and rhythm are sought where dialogue carries the meaning Rhyme and rhythm belong to poetry, not to the play the class is reading. This option reflects the common misconception that the features of one genre transfer to another. Teaching students to look for sound patterns in dialogue will not help them read a script.

subject: Teaching Reading
stem: After a read-aloud, Ms. Boyd asks her first graders to retell the story. One student says, 'The dog ran away, and then he found the boy, and I liked the part with the mud puddle.' Which statement best characterizes this retell?
choices: The student comprehends the story well but has weak decoding skills
The student has confused the narrator's point of view with the author's
The student is summarizing too briefly because of limited working memory
The student recalls a central event and adds a personal reaction but does not yet sort central events from interesting details
correct_answer: The student recalls a central event and adds a personal reaction but does not yet sort central events from interesting details
explanation: The question requires an understanding of how to support students in identifying central ideas and key details. The student produces one event that matters to the plot and then drifts to a favorite moment, which is typical of early retelling. The instructional need is a routine for deciding which events the story cannot do without.

distractor_explanations.The student comprehends the story well b: Attributing a weakness in oral retelling to decoding, even though retelling a read-aloud involves no print at all The retell is oral, so decoding never enters into it. This option reflects the common misconception that any reading difficulty signals a decoding problem. Because the student is retelling a story that was read aloud, the evidence points to comprehension and selection, not to word attack.
distractor_explanations.The student has confused the narrator's: Reading a student's personal reaction to a story as confusion about point of view or about who is speaking Adding a personal reaction is not an error about who is speaking. This option reflects the common misconception that student involvement with a text signals confusion about perspective. The student knows the story was told to her; she is simply reporting enjoyment alongside recall.
distractor_explanations.The student is summarizing too briefly b: Attributing poor selection of events to limited working memory, when the missing skill is judging which events matter most Length is not the problem; the retell contains enough content, but that content is not weighted by importance. This option reflects the common misconception that a thin retell indicates a capacity limit. Teaching students to rank events by importance addresses the selection problem, which more memory would not solve.

subject: Teaching Reading
stem: Ms. Nakamura's fourth graders are reading a folktale from a culture unfamiliar to most of the class, and several students misinterpret the characters' motives. Which combination of steps best supports comprehension while respecting students' cultural backgrounds?
choices: Building relevant background knowledge before reading and using a graphic organizer to track characters' motives during reading
Replacing the folktale with a story set in the students' own community
Explaining to students that characters in traditional tales act for reasons modern readers cannot understand
Having students read the folktale silently twice and then write a summary
correct_answer: Building relevant background knowledge before reading and using a graphic organizer to track characters' motives during reading
explanation: The question requires an understanding of how to differentiate instruction for learners from varied cultural backgrounds. Supplying the knowledge the tale assumes and giving students a structure for recording what characters want and why supports comprehension without lowering the task or replacing the text, so students keep their access to a tradition not their own.

distractor_explanations.Replacing the folktale with a story set: Treating unfamiliar cultural content as a reason to replace the text rather than to supply the knowledge the text assumes Swapping the text removes the opportunity to learn about another culture rather than making the original comprehensible. This option reflects the common misconception that the respectful response to unfamiliar content is to avoid it. The difficulty here is missing knowledge, and knowledge can be taught.
distractor_explanations.Explaining to students that characters i: Treating cultural distance as making a text unreadable, which closes off the inference the lesson should invite Declaring the motives inaccessible tells students that inference is impossible here and shuts down the thinking the lesson should provoke. This option reflects the common misconception that cultural distance makes interpretation inappropriate. Readers can learn to reason about unfamiliar values once they have enough information about them.
distractor_explanations.Having students read the folktale silent: Treating repeated silent reading as differentiation for comprehension difficulty, when the gap is missing context from outside the text Silent rereading adds exposure but no new knowledge or structure, so students will most likely reproduce the same misreadings. This option reflects the common misconception that repetition compensates for missing information. Comprehension fails here for lack of context, which must come from outside the text.

subject: Teaching Reading
stem: A second-grade teacher devotes fifteen minutes daily to writing instruction: she models a sentence pattern, writes one sentence with the class, then has students write several independently while she checks letter formation and spelling. Which principle best explains why this routine is effective?
choices: Writing improves fastest when teachers comment only on ideas, because mechanics take care of themselves over time
Writing develops through systematic, explicit instruction, and transcription skills must be taught directly so that handwriting and spelling become automatic enough to free attention for composing
Writing develops naturally from wide reading, so the teacher's main job is to give students time to write
Writing instruction should begin with whole-text composition, because young children already form letters fluently
correct_answer: Writing develops through systematic, explicit instruction, and transcription skills must be taught directly so that handwriting and spelling become automatic enough to free attention for composing
explanation: The question requires an understanding of systematic, explicit writing instruction for all learners. Modeling, shared writing, and guided practice make the sentence pattern visible before students attempt it alone, and attending to letter formation and spelling builds the transcription fluency that keeps young writers from spending all their working memory on forming letters instead of on what they want to say.

distractor_explanations.Writing improves fastest when teachers c: Treating feedback on ideas alone as the way to protect young writers, on the assumption that attention to conventions harms expression Mechanics do not resolve themselves for many students, and ignoring them leaves struggling writers without the feedback they need. This option reflects the common misconception that attention to conventions damages young writers' ideas. Explicit attention to both is what allows ideas to reach the page legibly.
distractor_explanations.Writing develops naturally from wide rea: Assuming that writing is absorbed naturally from reading and practice time, so explicit teaching of its components is unnecessary Writing is not absorbed from reading; its components must be taught. This option reflects the common misconception that literacy skills transfer from input alone. Reading supplies models and knowledge, but sentence construction, spelling, and planning each require explicit teaching and practice.
distractor_explanations.Writing instruction should begin with wh: Treating transcription as a prerequisite young writers already have, rather than as a skill that competes with ideas for attention Most second graders are still building handwriting and spelling automaticity, which is exactly why this teacher checks them. This option reflects the common misconception that transcription is a prerequisite already in place by the time composing begins. When transcription is slow, it competes with ideas for attention.

subject: Teaching Reading
stem: Ms. Alvarez's third graders draft personal narratives, conference with her, and then use a short checklist to decide what to change before writing a new version. Which feature of this routine best reflects writing as a recursive process?
choices: Students receive a score after each draft so they know how well they performed
Students start a brand-new topic each week, so they gain practice with many kinds of writing
Students return to an existing draft to revise it based on their own evaluation instead of treating a finished paper as final
Students copy a corrected version of their draft in their best handwriting for display
correct_answer: Students return to an existing draft to revise it based on their own evaluation instead of treating a finished paper as final
explanation: The question requires an understanding of how to teach writing as a recursive process. Revision, editing, and rewriting are not a cleanup stage that happens once at the end; writers move back and forth among planning, drafting, and revising as their ideas develop. Having students evaluate their own draft with a checklist and then re-enter it to make changes puts the loop into the routine rather than leaving it as advice.

distractor_explanations.Students receive a score after each draf: Assuming that grading motivates revision; evaluation that supports recursion must be criterion-referenced and student-directed, not a summary judgment. A score reports how a performance was judged but does not tell students what to change or invite them back into the text. Self-evaluation against criteria, not the mark itself, is what drives the next draft.
distractor_explanations.Students start a brand-new topic each we: Treating writing production as the goal and equating a high output of finished pieces with recursive process writing. Producing a new piece each week increases volume but keeps the process linear: each text is started, finished, and abandoned. Nothing leads students back into a text they have already written.
distractor_explanations.Students copy a corrected version of the: Confusing neat handwriting and a clean final copy with the intellectual work of revising; this reduces writing to handwriting and spelling. Copying a corrected draft is transcription, not revision. It changes the appearance of the paper without asking students to reconsider meaning, organization, or word choice.

subject: Teaching Reading
stem: A second-grade teacher plans a unit in which students write about something that happened to them, including what they felt and why it mattered. Which genre is the teacher introducing?
choices: Descriptive, because students use sensory details about people and places
Opinion/argumentative, because students state what they think about their experience
Informative/explanatory, because students convey information about an event
Narrative, because students recount an experience and convey its personal significance
correct_answer: Narrative, because students recount an experience and convey its personal significance
explanation: The question requires an understanding of how common writing genres are taught. Narrative writing recounts a sequence of events and conveys what the experience meant to the writer. Asking students to include what they felt and why the event mattered is what separates a narrative recount from a bare report of what happened.

distractor_explanations.Descriptive, because students use sensor: Identifying genre from a local surface feature instead of the overall communicative purpose of the piece. Sensory detail is a technique that appears inside many genres, including narrative. The presence of description does not make description the genre, and the unit described asks for an event and its significance, not a still portrait of a person or place.
distractor_explanations.Opinion/argumentative, because students: Treating any statement of personal preference or feeling as argument; argument requires a contestable claim plus reasons directed at an audience. Opinion writing asks students to take a position on a debatable question and support it with reasons aimed at a reader who may disagree. Expressing feeling about a personal experience is not the same as arguing a claim.
distractor_explanations.Informative/explanatory, because student: Judging genre by subject matter rather than by the writer's purpose; an event can appear in both an explanation and a story, and purpose is what distinguishes them. Informative writing exists to explain or inform a reader about a topic, using facts, definitions, and examples. Telling what happened to the writer, with the writer's reaction at the center, serves a different purpose.

subject: Teaching Reading
stem: A first-grade teacher is teaching the -ck spelling for /k/ at the end of a short-vowel word. Which pairing of activities best uses decoding and encoding as reciprocal skills?
choices: Students read a list of -ck words aloud, then reread the same list to build speed
Students read -ck words in a decodable passage, then use sound boxes to spell those same words and check their spelling against the text
Students match pictures to printed -ck words, then draw a picture for one of the words
Students listen for final /k/ in spoken words, then sort pictures by whether the word ends in /k/
correct_answer: Students read -ck words in a decodable passage, then use sound boxes to spell those same words and check their spelling against the text
explanation: The question requires an understanding of how decoding and encoding reinforce each other. Reading the words in print and then spelling those very same words sends students over identical letter sequences in both directions, and checking the spelling against the text makes the correspondence explicit. Each process strengthens the mental representation the other depends on, which is why the two taught together produce more growth than either taught alone.

distractor_explanations.Students read a list of -ck words aloud,: Mistaking repeated reading in one direction for a reciprocal routine; fluency practice does not exercise encoding at all. Both halves of this pairing run in the reading direction. Rereading for speed builds automaticity, which is valuable, but no part of it asks students to go from sound to print.
distractor_explanations.Students match pictures to printed -ck w: Assuming that any activity involving printed words exercises encoding; encoding requires segmenting and mapping sounds to letters, not recognizing a word. Matching pictures to words and drawing require students to connect print to meaning, not to analyze the sound structure and reconstruct the spelling. The phoneme-by-grapheme work that constitutes encoding is absent.
distractor_explanations.Students listen for final /k/ in spoken: Selecting an activity at the wrong level of the literacy hierarchy; oral sound work precedes and does not substitute for print-based reading and writing. Listening for a sound and sorting pictures is phonemic awareness: it operates entirely on speech with no print. It is a sensible precursor, but it sits below both decoding and encoding and cannot link them.

subject: Teaching Reading
stem: A fourth-grade teacher devotes part of each week to helping students learn new words well enough to use them in their own talk and classroom discussion, before the students meet those words in print. Which statement best explains why building oral vocabulary in this way supports reading comprehension?
choices: A word already known in speech becomes meaningful the moment it is decoded in print, so oral vocabulary sets the ceiling on what an accurate decoder can understand
Using new words in spoken sentences gives students more practice sounding out unfamiliar print, and decoding remains the main barrier to comprehension in fourth grade
Hearing words used in conversation teaches students to work out meanings from context, so the oral work mainly builds a strategy for handling unfamiliar words
Once students decode accurately, comprehension takes care of itself, so oral vocabulary work mainly helps students who still struggle with word reading
correct_answer: A word already known in speech becomes meaningful the moment it is decoded in print, so oral vocabulary sets the ceiling on what an accurate decoder can understand
explanation: The question requires an understanding of how oral language comprehension supports reading comprehension. Reading comprehension depends on both accurate word reading and language comprehension. A word a student already knows when hearing it carries its meaning into print, so decoding it delivers meaning at once; a word that is decoded but has no entry in the student's oral vocabulary yields sound without sense. Oral vocabulary therefore sets the ceiling on how much of a text accurate decoding can deliver.

distractor_explanations.Using new words in spoken sentences give: Treating oral vocabulary work as decoding practice and assuming word reading is still the primary barrier to comprehension in the upper elementary grades Saying and hearing new words gives students practice with spoken language, not with print-to-sound mapping, so it does not build decoding. By fourth grade, students who already read accurately are usually limited by word meaning rather than by word reading, which is exactly why the teacher turned to oral vocabulary.
distractor_explanations.Hearing words used in conversation teach: Mistaking a by-product of vocabulary instruction, such as using context clues, for the reason vocabulary supports comprehension, rather than direct knowledge of word meanings Students may indeed become better at guessing unknown words from context, but that is a side effect rather than the mechanism at work. The gain comes from knowing more words outright, so that fewer words are unknown in the first place. A strategy for coping with unfamiliar words cannot substitute for knowing them.
distractor_explanations.Once students decode accurately, compreh: Assuming comprehension follows automatically once decoding is accurate, so that language comprehension places no limit on reading comprehension Accurate decoding does not produce understanding on its own; a reader who sounds out every word still has to bring language comprehension to the page. This statement also wrongly confines oral vocabulary work to struggling readers, when it is precisely what allows accurate decoders to make sense of the words they read.

subject: Teaching Reading
stem: A fourth-grade teacher models pausing at the end of each section of an informational text to jot down one question the section raised for her, then has students jot down their own questions and check whether later sections answer them. Which comprehension strategy is the teacher primarily teaching?
choices: Clarifying, because students stop where the text stops making sense and use a fix-up strategy to restore meaning
Summarizing, because students reduce each section to its most important ideas and set aside minor details
Questioning, because students generate their own questions about the text and look for answers as they read on
Making connections, because students link what they are reading to their own experiences and to other texts
correct_answer: Questioning, because students generate their own questions about the text and look for answers as they read on
explanation: The question requires an understanding of instructional strategies that improve comprehension. The teacher is showing students how to turn their own curiosity about a text into questions and then to keep reading with those questions in mind. Generating questions and hunting for answers keeps readers actively building meaning instead of moving passively through the text, which is why self-questioning is taught as a strategy in its own right.

distractor_explanations.Clarifying, because students stop where: Confusing a pause to record a question with a pause because comprehension has broken down; clarifying responds to lost meaning, while questioning responds to curiosity Clarifying is triggered by a breakdown in understanding: the reader notices that meaning has been lost and applies a fix such as rereading or reading ahead. Nothing in this lesson signals confusion. Students are asking about content they do understand in order to find out more, so the demand is curiosity rather than repair.
distractor_explanations.Summarizing, because students reduce eac: Treating any written response to a section of text as summarizing; summarizing is defined by selecting and condensing content, not by raising questions about it Summarizing asks students to decide what matters across a stretch of text and condense it, dropping the rest. Students here are producing questions, not condensed statements, and they read forward to see whether an answer appears rather than looking back over what they have already read.
distractor_explanations.Making connections, because students lin: Assuming that any active response to reading involves relating the text to personal experience or other books; questioning keeps students working with the text's own content Making connections asks students to bring something from outside the text, such as a personal experience or another book, and link it to what they are reading. The questions in this lesson are answered from the text itself, so students are working within the text rather than connecting it to anything beyond it.

subject: Teaching Reading
stimulus: A fourth-grade class reads the sentence: "The old house groaned as the wind pushed against its loose shutters."
stem: Which question best develops students' understanding of why the author wrote that the house "groaned"?
choices: "What is the dictionary definition of groaned, and what part of speech is it?"
"Who is speaking in this sentence, and what do we know about that character?"
"What sound does groaned describe, and how would you say it out loud?"
"Can a house really groan? What is the author comparing the house to, and what feeling does that comparison create?"
correct_answer: "Can a house really groan? What is the author comparing the house to, and what feeling does that comparison create?"
explanation: The question requires an understanding of how to teach figurative language. Having students notice that a house cannot literally groan, then identify what is being compared and what mood the comparison creates, moves them from a literal reading to the author's purpose. That three-part move — notice the impossibility, name the comparison, explain the effect — is the core of instruction in figurative language.

distractor_explanations.\"What is the dictionary definition of g: Treating figurative language as a vocabulary problem; teaching the denotation does not explain the comparison or its effect. A literal definition cannot account for the author's choice, because the point of the word here is precisely that it does not apply literally. Treating it as an unknown vocabulary word misses the device.
distractor_explanations.\"Who is speaking in this sentence, and: Applying a different literary lens to the passage; point of view and character analysis do not address how the comparison builds meaning. This question asks about speaker and characterization, which is a different literary element. The sentence's figurative force comes from the comparison, not from who is talking.
distractor_explanations.\"What sound does groaned describe, and: Substituting performance of the text for analysis of it; expressive reading is a fluency outcome, not figurative language comprehension. Asking students to produce the sound addresses oral reading and expression. It keeps attention on how the word is performed rather than on what the comparison means.

subject: Teaching Reading
stem: Before reading a short play, a fourth-grade teacher introduces the terms dialogue, scene, and stage directions with student-friendly definitions, several examples and non-examples, and a wall chart students will use while reading. Which evaluation of this approach is most accurate?
choices: It is misguided, because vocabulary of this kind is best acquired incidentally through wide reading rather than taught directly
It gives students direct instruction in the labels they need to notice, discuss, and analyze the structural features that carry meaning in a play
It will work only if students memorize the definitions before reading, because knowing definitions is what determines comprehension
It removes the need to teach comprehension strategies, because once students know the terms they will understand the play
correct_answer: It gives students direct instruction in the labels they need to notice, discuss, and analyze the structural features that carry meaning in a play
explanation: The question requires an understanding of how direct vocabulary instruction supports comprehension of genre features. Terms such as scene and stage directions name the structures that carry a play's meaning: stage directions tell readers what a spectator would see, and scene boundaries signal shifts in time and place. Teaching these words directly with examples and non-examples gives students the language to talk about the structure, and explicit teaching of this kind is more efficient than leaving such low-frequency academic terms to incidental acquisition.

distractor_explanations.It is misguided, because vocabulary of t: Assuming all vocabulary is best acquired incidentally through wide reading; direct instruction is indicated for academic and text-structure terms. Incidental acquisition from wide reading is too slow and too uneven for low-frequency academic and genre-specific terms, and students who most need the words encounter them least. Direct instruction is the recommended route for precisely this vocabulary.
distractor_explanations.It will work only if students memorize t: Equating direct vocabulary instruction with definition drill; robust word knowledge requires depth of processing, not verbatim recall. Memorized definitions produce knowledge of a label without the ability to use it. Effective direct instruction goes beyond the definition to multiple examples, non-examples, and repeated use in reading and discussion.
distractor_explanations.It removes the need to teach comprehensi: Treating vocabulary knowledge as a replacement for comprehension strategies; vocabulary supports meaning construction but does not substitute for it. Words are tools that let students talk about and attend to structure; they do not do the work of making inferences, tracking events, or integrating ideas. Comprehension strategy instruction is still required.

subject: Teaching Reading
stem: Before reading a complex informational article about animal migration with her second graders, Ms. Reyes previews three key terms, shows photographs, and leads a brief discussion of why animals move from place to place. Which statement best explains the purpose of this routine?
choices: It lowers the cognitive load of the text so students can spend attention on constructing meaning and using comprehension strategies
It guarantees that students will not meet any unfamiliar words while they read
It converts the lesson from reading instruction into science instruction, which is more concrete for young students
It lets the teacher skip comprehension strategy instruction because the content has already been explained
correct_answer: It lowers the cognitive load of the text so students can spend attention on constructing meaning and using comprehension strategies
explanation: The question requires an understanding of how prereading supports work with complex text. Preteaching a small set of high-utility words and activating the key concept supplies part of the knowledge the text assumes, so less of the reader's limited working memory is spent on word recognition and unfamiliar ideas. The attention freed up can go to integrating information and applying strategies such as questioning and summarizing.

distractor_explanations.It guarantees that students will not mee: Expecting prereading vocabulary work to eliminate unknown words; its function is to build the knowledge base the text presupposes, not to exhaust the vocabulary. Previewing three words cannot remove every unfamiliar word, and that is not the aim. The aim is to equip students with the concepts the text leans on and with strategies for handling words that remain unknown.
distractor_explanations.It converts the lesson from reading inst: Mistaking background-knowledge building for a change of subject; concept discussion is a comprehension support, not an abandonment of reading instruction. Discussing the concept serves the reading: it supplies the background knowledge the article assumes. The lesson remains a reading lesson, and the content knowledge is mobilized in service of comprehension.
distractor_explanations.It lets the teacher skip comprehension s: Treating prereading preparation as a substitute for strategy instruction; scaffolding before reading reduces load but does not replace guidance during reading. Preliminary support prepares students to read but does not do the reading for them. Students still need strategy instruction during and after reading to handle the parts of the text that remain demanding.

subject: Teaching Reading
stem: A third-grade teacher asks students to retell a story in exactly four sentences: who the character was, what the character wanted, what went wrong, and how it ended. Which skill does this activity primarily develop?
choices: Reading fluency, because students practice saying the story aloud
Phonemic awareness, because students think about the sounds in words
Identifying the main idea and key details, because students must choose the most important elements and leave the rest out
Decoding multisyllabic words, because students meet new words while they retell
correct_answer: Identifying the main idea and key details, because students must choose the most important elements and leave the rest out
explanation: The question requires an understanding of how to support students in identifying central ideas and key details. A constrained retell forces a decision about what matters: with only four sentences and four specified elements, students cannot include everything, so they must rank information and cite the specific details that carry the story. That act of selecting and supporting is the same judgment required to state a main idea with evidence.

distractor_explanations.Reading fluency, because students practi: Equating oral production with fluency; retelling requires reconstructing meaning, whereas fluency concerns accuracy, rate, and prosody in reading visible text. Fluency practice means reading text accurately and expressively from the page. A retell asks students to put the text away and generate their own sentences, which is a comprehension task, not a reading-rate task.
distractor_explanations.Phonemic awareness, because students thi: Placing a meaning-level comprehension task at the word-sound level; the activity makes no demand on attention to individual phonemes. Phonemic awareness operates on the sound structure of spoken words and is typically developed well before third grade. A retell addresses meaning at the level of the whole text.
distractor_explanations.Decoding multisyllabic words, because st: Confusing an incidental demand of an activity with its instructional target; the task is defined by the decisions about content it requires. Decoding may occur incidentally, but nothing in the task directs attention to print. Retelling works from memory of meaning rather than from words on the page.

subject: Teaching Reading
stem: In a fifth-grade class reading the same work of historical fiction, several students are losing track of the large cast of characters and their relationships. Which adaptation best supports their comprehension?
choices: Have the struggling students take turns reading the novel aloud to build fluency
Give the struggling students a list of comprehension questions to answer on their own after reading
Assign the struggling students a shorter, simpler text on a different topic so that they have less to read
Have the whole class use a character relationship graphic organizer, and complete part of it together with the struggling students before they work on their own
correct_answer: Have the whole class use a character relationship graphic organizer, and complete part of it together with the struggling students before they work on their own
explanation: The question requires an understanding of how to differentiate instruction for diverse learners. A graphic organizer externalizes the relationships that the students are failing to hold in mind, and completing part of it with the teacher supplies scaffolding that is faded as students take over. Keeping the whole class on the same text preserves access to the shared discussion and to grade-level content, which is what makes the support differentiated rather than simply reduced.

distractor_explanations.Have the struggling students take turns: Applying a fluency routine to a comprehension problem; the diagnosis points to holding and organizing information, not to reading accuracy. Oral reading turns do not address the stated difficulty, which is tracking relationships among characters. Round-robin reading also gives each student little actual reading practice.
distractor_explanations.Give the struggling students a list of c: Mistaking independent practice for scaffolding; assigning harder work without support is the opposite of differentiation. Independent questions after reading remove support at the point where these students need it most and provide no information until the reading is over. The students need guidance while they construct meaning, not a check afterward.
distractor_explanations.Assign the struggling students a shorter: Equating differentiation with an easier text; differentiating means changing support and representation, not lowering the content ceiling. Moving these students to a simpler text on another topic lowers both the challenge and the content. They lose the vocabulary, knowledge, and participation in class discussion that the novel provides, and the gap widens.

subject: Teaching Reading
stem: A fourth-grade teacher models reading a difficult paragraph by saying aloud, "This sentence doesn't make sense to me. I'm going to reread the sentence before it to see what 'it' refers to." Which statement best describes the purpose of this think-aloud?
choices: It models fluent oral reading so that students can imitate the teacher's expression
It makes the normally invisible process of monitoring comprehension and choosing a fix-up strategy visible to students
It supplies background knowledge about the topic of the paragraph
It assesses whether students can answer literal questions about the text
correct_answer: It makes the normally invisible process of monitoring comprehension and choosing a fix-up strategy visible to students
explanation: The question requires an understanding of how to model and guide metacognitive monitoring. Skilled readers notice when meaning breaks down and act to repair it, but both steps happen silently. By voicing the moment of confusion and the specific repair chosen, the teacher makes an internal process observable, and repeated modeling of this kind is what allows students to take over the strategy for themselves.

distractor_explanations.It models fluent oral reading so that st: Reducing a think-aloud to a reading model; the point is to externalize cognition, not to demonstrate prosody. Expression and phrasing are fluency outcomes. The content of this think-aloud is a comprehension problem and a repair, and its value lies in exposing thinking rather than in providing a reading performance to copy.
distractor_explanations.It supplies background knowledge about t: Confusing strategy modeling with content scaffolding; think-alouds teach a process that transfers across topics rather than knowledge of this one. The teacher says nothing about the topic. What is being demonstrated is what to do when comprehension fails, which applies to any topic and any paragraph.
distractor_explanations.It assesses whether students can answer: Mistaking a demonstration for an assessment opportunity; modeling precedes and supports performance rather than measuring it. No student performance is being sampled here. Modeling comes before independent practice and is designed to build the strategy, whereas assessment would call for students to demonstrate it while the teacher observes.

subject: Teaching Reading
stem: According to the Not-So-Simple View of Writing, which statement best explains why systematic, explicit writing instruction is necessary?
choices: Ideas come first; transcription skills should be taught only after students can generate text freely
Writing is speech written down, so once students can talk about a topic they can write about it
Writing draws on transcription, on idea generation, and on self-regulation at the same time, and these compete for limited working memory, so each needs explicit teaching
Writing develops naturally out of reading, so explicit instruction is needed only for handwriting and spelling
correct_answer: Writing draws on transcription, on idea generation, and on self-regulation at the same time, and these compete for limited working memory, so each needs explicit teaching
explanation: The question requires an understanding of systematic, explicit writing instruction. The Not-So-Simple View holds that writing is constrained by transcription, by text generation, and by the executive functions that plan, draft, and revise, all drawing on the same limited working memory. Because unautomated transcription consumes capacity that would otherwise go to ideas, and because planning and revision are not picked up incidentally, each component must be taught explicitly and systematically.

distractor_explanations.Ideas come first; transcription skills s: Sequencing writing components strictly rather than developing them together; unautomated transcription constrains composition from the start. Delaying transcription instruction leaves students struggling with letter formation and spelling at exactly the moment they are trying to compose, which drains working memory. Automating transcription early is what frees capacity for ideas.
distractor_explanations.Writing is speech written down, so once: Holding the Simple View that writing is spoken language written down; this ignores the planning and self-regulation demands unique to writing. This is the Simple View, which treats writing as the transcription of speech and has been superseded. Writing places demands that speech does not, including spelling, punctuation, and the management of a longer, unsupported stretch of language.
distractor_explanations.Writing develops naturally out of readin: Assuming writing is a by-product of reading and that only handwriting and spelling need teaching; this neglects idea generation and self-regulation. Reading supports writing but does not teach it automatically. Transcription is one component of a larger set, and text generation and self-regulated revision require their own instruction.

subject: Teaching Reading
stem: After a small-group lesson on making inferences, Ms. Ortiz asks each student to write one sentence naming an inference they made and the sentence from the text that led to it. She reads the slips before forming the next day's groups. Which evaluation of this activity is most accurate?
choices: It is an informal formative assessment that makes students' thinking visible, so she can see whether they are grounding inferences in text evidence and regroup accordingly
It is an informal assessment, but it measures writing mechanics rather than comprehension, so it cannot guide reading instruction
It is a formal summative assessment because it produces a written product that can be scored
It is mainly a comprehension strategy lesson, and its usefulness ends once students have filled in the slip
correct_answer: It is an informal formative assessment that makes students' thinking visible, so she can see whether they are grounding inferences in text evidence and regroup accordingly
explanation: The question requires an understanding of how to evaluate instructional activities for the thinking they reveal. Asking for both the inference and the supporting sentence requires students to show their reasoning rather than only their answer, which lets the teacher distinguish a student who guessed from one who used evidence. Because the slips are read immediately and used to form the next day's groups, the activity functions formatively: it is ungraded, quick, and directly changes what happens next.

distractor_explanations.It is an informal assessment, but it mea: Judging an assessment by the format of the response instead of by the construct it samples; the response mode does not determine what is measured. Writing is the vehicle here, not the object. The teacher reads the slips for the relationship between claim and evidence, and a slip with weak mechanics can still show sound reasoning, or the reverse.
distractor_explanations.It is a formal summative assessment beca: Treating any written, scoreable product as formal and summative; the distinguishing feature is how the results are used, not their physical form. Formal summative assessment uses standardized administration and scoring to report achievement after instruction. This exit slip has no scoring rubric, is administered by the classroom teacher, and is used to adjust tomorrow's teaching, all of which make it informal and formative.
distractor_explanations.It is mainly a comprehension strategy le: Seeing an assessment encounter only as practice; the same activity can both develop thinking and yield data, and the data should drive instruction. The activity does give students practice, but the teacher collects and reads the slips for a reason. Overlooking the information they carry discards the evidence that should shape the next lesson.

subject: Teaching Reading
stimulus: A fifth-grade class reads two poems about the same school playground: one written from the point of view of a student who has just transferred to the school, and one written from the point of view of the oldest tree on the grounds.
stem: Which statement best explains why teaching point of view supports comprehension?
choices: Point of view appears only in fiction, so it has little bearing on understanding most texts
Identifying point of view is mainly a way to sort texts into genres before reading
Point of view matters chiefly because comprehension questions ask students to name the narrator
Point of view establishes who is speaking and what that speaker is in a position to know, so recognizing it lets students judge the limits and reliability of what is presented
correct_answer: Point of view establishes who is speaking and what that speaker is in a position to know, so recognizing it lets students judge the limits and reliability of what is presented
explanation: The question requires an understanding of how teaching literary devices improves comprehension of text. Point of view fixes the position from which events are filtered, and that position determines what the speaker can observe and what interests shape the telling. Once students identify who is speaking, they can ask what this speaker would not know or would report differently, which is what allows them to read the same event critically in two poems.

distractor_explanations.Point of view appears only in fiction, s: Restricting point of view to fiction; perspective and stance shape the presentation of information in nonfiction as well. Point of view operates in nonfiction as well, where the author's stance and sources shape what is reported and what is omitted. Dismissing it as a fiction-only feature leaves students without a tool for evaluating informational texts.
distractor_explanations.Identifying point of view is mainly a wa: Treating a literary device as a labeling exercise; the value of point of view lies in explaining how the telling is constrained, not in classifying texts. Genre classification may be a by-product, but the reason to teach point of view is that it explains how information is filtered. Sorting texts does not require students to use the concept while reading.
distractor_explanations.Point of view matters chiefly because co: Justifying literature instruction by test formats; devices are taught for the interpretive work they enable. Naming the narrator is a recall task that can be done without any effect on interpretation. The device is taught because it changes what the reader takes the text to mean.

subject: Teaching Reading
stem: A second-grade teacher is preparing students to read a short play. Which structural feature most directly helps students understand where and when the events take place?
choices: The cast of characters listed at the beginning
The scene headings and stage directions that describe the setting
The dialogue spoken by the characters
The punctuation at the end of each line of dialogue
correct_answer: The scene headings and stage directions that describe the setting
explanation: The question requires an understanding of how the structural elements of a genre contribute to a text's meaning. In a play there is no narration to establish time and place, so that information is carried by the scene headings and stage directions. Teaching students to read these parts tells them where to look for the setting that the characters' words take for granted.

distractor_explanations.The cast of characters listed at the beg: Expecting one structural element to do the work of another; the cast list identifies participants, not circumstances. The cast list tells students who appears and sometimes how characters are related, but it does not establish the time or place of the action.
distractor_explanations.The dialogue spoken by the characters: Overlooking that in drama the setting is supplied outside the spoken lines; dialogue presumes a setting rather than establishing it. Dialogue advances the plot and reveals characters, and characters may mention where they are, but the play's own signal of time and place is the stage direction rather than the speech.
distractor_explanations.The punctuation at the end of each line: Confusing cues for oral delivery with cues for setting; punctuation guides expression, while stage directions carry the scene information. Punctuation at the end of a line indicates how the line should be delivered, such as whether it is a question or an exclamation. It carries performance information, not information about time or place.

subject: Teaching Reading
stem: Before a fifth-grade class reads a complex persuasive editorial, the teacher leads a discussion of the issue, has students list what they already know and what they question about it, and previews the signal words that mark a claim and its supporting reasons. Which statement best explains why this approach supports comprehension of the complex text?
choices: It activates and builds background knowledge and gives students a purpose for reading, which reduces the demands the text places on working memory
It ensures that students will agree with the author's opinion before they begin reading
It allows students to read the text without using any comprehension strategies
It effectively shortens the text, and length is the main reason complex texts are difficult
correct_answer: It activates and builds background knowledge and gives students a purpose for reading, which reduces the demands the text places on working memory
explanation: The question requires an understanding of how to support students' reading of complex text. Discussing the issue and recording what students know and question activates relevant knowledge and sets a purpose, so readers meet the text with a framework to attach new information to. Previewing the signal words for claims and reasons adds a structural roadmap, and together these reduce the load on working memory enough for students to attend to the argument itself.

distractor_explanations.It ensures that students will agree with: Confusing comprehension of a position with agreement with it; understanding an argument does not require accepting its conclusion. The goal is for students to understand the position and how it is supported, not to adopt it. Good readers can summarize and evaluate an argument they reject, and instruction protects that distinction.
distractor_explanations.It allows students to read the text with: Treating scaffolding as a replacement for strategy use; supports before reading reduce load but do not perform the comprehension work. Preliminary work prepares students to use strategies more effectively; it does not make strategies unnecessary. Students still need to question, monitor, and summarize as they work through the editorial's reasoning.
distractor_explanations.It effectively shortens the text, and le: Attributing text complexity to length; difficulty is driven mainly by concepts, vocabulary, and structure. Nothing about the text's length changes. What makes it complex is concept density, unfamiliar vocabulary, and the structure of the argument, and the teacher's moves target those rather than the number of words.

subject: Teaching Reading
stem: A third-grade teacher is preparing students to read a science article about ecosystems. The article contains the words "habitat," "predator," and "organism." Which instructional approach best supports students' comprehension of the article?
choices: Scheduling a vocabulary quiz on the words for the following week
Having students look up each word in a dictionary and copy the definition into a notebook
Preteaching the words with student-friendly definitions, examples, and non-examples before reading
Encouraging students to skip unfamiliar words and rely on context clues as they read
correct_answer: Preteaching the words with student-friendly definitions, examples, and non-examples before reading
explanation: The question requires an understanding of how to help students acquire common and domain-specific words through direct instruction. Domain-specific terms carry dense conceptual meaning, and preteaching them with accessible definitions plus examples and non-examples builds the background knowledge students need before they encounter the terms in text. Addressing them in advance means working memory during reading goes to comprehension rather than to decoding unfamiliar vocabulary.

distractor_explanations.Scheduling a vocabulary quiz on the word: Confusing assessment with instruction, as though scheduling a quiz were the same as teaching the words. A quiz is an assessment, and it is scheduled after the reading. It neither builds the knowledge needed to comprehend the article nor provides the instruction that would produce it.
distractor_explanations.Having students look up each word in a d: Equating completion of a vocabulary task with construction of the concept. Copying a definition produces a page of writing, not a usable meaning. Copying dictionary definitions is a clerical task rather than concept building. Dictionary entries are often written above students' reading levels and give multiple senses without guidance about which one applies, so students can complete the task without being able to use the words while reading.
distractor_explanations.Encouraging students to skip unfamiliar: Treating context clues as a strategy that works under any conditions. Inference needs partial knowledge and redundant surrounding text, and clustered technical terms supply neither. Context clues work best when students already have partial knowledge of a word and surrounding text is rich enough to constrain its meaning. With three dense domain-specific terms appearing together, students lack both prerequisites, so skipping them leaves the central concepts of the article inaccessible.

subject: Teaching Reading
stem: A teacher notices that a student reads a grade-level passage word by word with little expression. Which instructional practice most directly addresses this student's need?
choices: Independent silent reading of progressively more challenging texts
Daily practice with phonics worksheets focusing on vowel patterns
Previewing the passage's vocabulary words before the student reads
Repeated reading of the same passage with feedback on phrasing and expression
correct_answer: Repeated reading of the same passage with feedback on phrasing and expression
explanation: The question requires an understanding of how prosody is developed. Word-by-word reading with flat expression is a prosody problem, and repeated reading of a short passage with targeted feedback on phrasing is a research-supported way to build both automaticity and expressive contour.

distractor_explanations.Independent silent reading of progressiv: Assuming that more reading practice automatically improves fluency. Practice without feedback can consolidate an ineffective habit, and harder text works against automaticity. Independent silent reading generates no model and no feedback, so a student who reads word by word is likely to keep doing so. Raising text difficulty also lowers the accuracy and automaticity that fluency depends on.
distractor_explanations.Daily practice with phonics worksheets f: Reaching for phonics instruction to remedy any reading difficulty. Instructional responses should follow from what the evidence shows the student can already do. The student is producing the words, so decoding is not the bottleneck. Additional work on vowel patterns targets a skill the student has already demonstrated and leaves the phrasing problem untouched.
distractor_explanations.Previewing the passage's vocabulary word: Confusing a comprehension support with a fluency intervention. The two target different components of reading. Preteaching vocabulary removes meaning obstacles and supports comprehension, but this student's problem is one of delivery rather than of word meaning. Knowing every word would not by itself produce phrased, expressive reading.

subject: Teaching Reading
stem: A teacher is preparing third graders to read a science text that contains the words "evaporate," "condense," and "precipitate." Which practice best supports their comprehension of the text?
choices: Having students copy the glossary definitions into their notebooks the day before reading
Providing direct instruction on the words with examples, student-generated examples, and discussion before reading
Telling students to rely on context clues to work out the words as they encounter them
Assigning the words as spelling homework for the week before the lesson
correct_answer: Providing direct instruction on the words with examples, student-generated examples, and discussion before reading
explanation: The question requires an understanding of how academic and domain-specific vocabulary is best taught. Explicit teaching that pairs a student-friendly definition with examples, student-generated examples, and discussion builds the concept rather than a verbal label, and preteaching frees attention for comprehension during reading.

distractor_explanations.Having students copy the glossary defini: Equating exposure plus transcription with learning. Reproduction of a definition is not evidence of conceptual understanding. Copying definitions is shallow contact with a word. It does not require students to connect the term to the concept, so they can finish the task and still be unable to use or recognize the idea in the text.
distractor_explanations.Telling students to rely on context clue: Overestimating context clues. Context is unreliable precisely for the technical terms that carry the main ideas of a science text. These three words are the concepts the text is built on, and informational text rarely supplies clues strong enough to derive them accurately. Guessing here produces misunderstanding of the very content being taught.
distractor_explanations.Assigning the words as spelling homework: Treating word study as spelling study. Knowing how to write a word and knowing what it means are separate outcomes. Spelling practice builds orthographic memory, not conceptual knowledge. A student who can spell 'precipitate' may still not know what it means when it appears in the passage.

subject: Teaching Reading
stem: Which statement best explains why vocabulary knowledge is essential to reading comprehension?
choices: Vocabulary instruction teaches students to use context clues effectively
Fluent readers decode automatically, which frees their attention to focus on word meanings
Comprehension is built from the meanings of words, so a reader who does not know the words cannot construct the meaning of the text
Students with larger vocabularies read more quickly, and greater speed produces better comprehension
correct_answer: Comprehension is built from the meanings of words, so a reader who does not know the words cannot construct the meaning of the text
explanation: The question requires an understanding of the relationship between vocabulary and comprehension. Meaning is constructed from the words on the page, so when word meanings are missing, comprehension breaks down at the word level before larger structures such as sentences or the passage as a whole can be built.

distractor_explanations.Vocabulary instruction teaches students: Identifying a secondary benefit of instruction as the underlying rationale for the construct itself. Using context clues is one useful strategy for handling unknown words, but it is a by-product of vocabulary work rather than the reason vocabulary matters. The core contribution of vocabulary is direct access to meaning.
distractor_explanations.Fluent readers decode automatically, whi: Substituting a true statement about fluency for an explanation of vocabulary. Being correct in itself is not the same as being responsive to the question. This statement is true, but it explains why automatic decoding supports comprehension, not why vocabulary is necessary. It answers a different question than the one asked.
distractor_explanations.Students with larger vocabularies read m: Treating reading speed as the mechanism that produces comprehension. Speed and comprehension are related but distinct outcomes. Rate is a marker of fluency, not a cause of understanding. A reader with a strong vocabulary who reads slowly can still comprehend well, and a fast reader who does not know the words will not.

subject: Teaching Reading
stem: A teacher wants to promote vocabulary development through direct instruction. Which activity best reflects that approach?
choices: Asking students to illustrate each new word in a personal picture dictionary
Posting the week's words on the word wall and quizzing students on Friday
Having students read widely on their own and look up any unfamiliar words they meet
Explicitly teaching word meanings with student-friendly definitions, examples, and multiple exposures across contexts
correct_answer: Explicitly teaching word meanings with student-friendly definitions, examples, and multiple exposures across contexts
explanation: The question requires an understanding of what distinguishes direct vocabulary instruction. Student-friendly definitions, worked examples, and repeated meaningful encounters across contexts are the three hallmarks of direct instruction, and together they move a word from unfamiliar to usable.

distractor_explanations.Asking students to illustrate each new w: Assuming that producing something for a word proves the meaning was taught. Drawing 'evidence' or 'compare' does not establish the concept. Illustrating works for concrete nouns and fails for the abstract academic words that most affect comprehension. It is also a production task that comes after learning, not a way of teaching meaning.
distractor_explanations.Posting the week's words on the word wal: Treating display and testing as instruction. Without explicit teaching of meaning, exposure alone produces weak and slow growth. A word wall and a Friday quiz provide exposure and measurement but no explicit explanation of meaning. Students may recognize the words by Friday and still be unable to use any of them.
distractor_explanations.Having students read widely on their own: Confusing incidental learning conditions with direct instruction. Indirect learning is valuable but insufficient on its own, particularly for struggling readers. Wide independent reading and self-directed lookup are valuable complements, but they are indirect routes to word learning. Students who most need vocabulary support are least likely to look words up accurately on their own.

subject: Teaching Reading
stem: A teacher wants students to be able to work out the meaning of an unfamiliar word they meet while reading. Which instructional practice best develops that ability?
choices: Modeling how to examine the surrounding words and sentences, the word's syntactic role, and its word parts
Encouraging students to skip unfamiliar words and keep reading for the main idea
Having students memorize a list of the text's difficult words before they read
Teaching students to consult the glossary first and use context only as a backup
correct_answer: Modeling how to examine the surrounding words and sentences, the word's syntactic role, and its word parts
explanation: The question requires an understanding of how word-solving strategies are taught. Deriving meaning draws on three sources at once: the semantic context in nearby words and sentences, the syntactic role the word plays, and morphological information from roots and affixes. Modeling all three teaches a procedure rather than an answer.

distractor_explanations.Encouraging students to skip unfamiliar: Confusing a coping behavior with a comprehension strategy. Getting past a word is not the same as getting its meaning. Skipping unknown words is avoidance, not inference. Missed words accumulate, and each gap weakens the reader's model of the text, so comprehension erodes as the passage goes on.
distractor_explanations.Having students memorize a list of the t: Mistaking coverage of a specific text's vocabulary for development of a transferable skill. Preteaching and memorizing the difficult words in one text helps with that text only. It gives students nothing to use when they meet an untaught word, which is the situation the question describes.
distractor_explanations.Teaching students to consult the glossar: Preferring an answer source over a strategy. The goal is for students to handle words nobody pre-selected for them. A glossary supplies the meaning of listed words but teaches no method, and it is useless for the many unlisted words a student will meet. Treating it as the first resort makes students dependent on it.

subject: Teaching Reading
stem: A second grader reads a grade-level passage accurately but slowly, one word at a time, pausing at the end of every line. Which statement best explains how this reading behavior is likely to affect comprehension?
choices: Accuracy guarantees that meaning is constructed, so comprehension is unlikely to be affected.
Effort spent identifying individual words leaves less attention available for constructing meaning from the text.
The behavior lowers comprehension only when the passage contains unfamiliar vocabulary.
Comprehension depends on the reader's background knowledge rather than on how the words are read.
correct_answer: Effort spent identifying individual words leaves less attention available for constructing meaning from the text.
explanation: The question requires an understanding of how fluency contributes to comprehension. When word recognition is not yet automatic, attention is consumed by identifying one word after another, so the beginning of the sentence is often lost before the end is reached. Accurate but labored reading therefore still leaves the reader with too little capacity left to build the meaning of the sentence and the passage.

distractor_explanations.Accuracy guarantees that meaning is cons: Treating accuracy and fluency as the same thing, with rate and automaticity as optional extras Option (A) is incorrect. Accurate decoding is one component of fluent reading, but on its own it does not free attention for meaning; a reader can identify every word correctly and still fail to hold the sentence together. This option reflects the common misconception that accuracy and fluency are the same thing, with rate and automaticity treated as optional extras.
distractor_explanations.The behavior lowers comprehension only w: Assuming fluency only matters in difficult texts, so that word-by-word reading of familiar material needs no attention Option (C) is incorrect. Unfamiliar vocabulary is one source of comprehension difficulty, but labored word recognition limits comprehension on its own, even in texts whose words are all familiar to the reader. This option reflects the common misconception that fluency only matters in hard texts, so a student who reads familiar material word by word is seen as having no problem to address.
distractor_explanations.Comprehension depends on the reader's ba: Assuming background knowledge can substitute for the mechanics of reading Option (D) is incorrect. Background knowledge does support comprehension, but it works alongside fluent word recognition rather than in place of it; a knowledgeable reader who must decode every word still loses the thread of the sentence. This option reflects the common misconception that background knowledge can substitute for the mechanics of reading.

subject: Teaching Reading
stem: A third-grade teacher wants students to read with appropriate expression, pausing at commas and raising pitch at question marks. Which instructional routine best develops this aspect of oral reading?
choices: Having students complete daily phoneme segmentation activities with counters
Timing students for one minute on a passage and graphing their words-correct-per-minute scores
Having students chorally read a short poem that the teacher has marked for phrasing and stress, then reread it with a partner
Having students practice reading lists of words that contain the week's vowel pattern
correct_answer: Having students chorally read a short poem that the teacher has marked for phrasing and stress, then reread it with a partner
explanation: The question requires an understanding of how to teach students to read orally with prosody. Marking the text makes phrase boundaries and stress visible, choral reading supplies a fluent model to imitate, and partner rereading gives students several attempts at producing the same phrasing. The target of the routine is expression, not speed.

distractor_explanations.Having students complete daily phoneme s: Assuming any foundational routine improves oral reading, without matching the routine to the level of the difficulty Option (D) is incorrect. Segmenting phonemes with counters is phonemic awareness work that operates on spoken words, well below the level of reading sentences aloud. This option reflects the common misconception that any foundational routine will improve oral reading, without matching the routine to the level of the difficulty.
distractor_explanations.Timing students for one minute on a pass: Treating rate as the whole of fluency, so that raising speed is assumed to produce expression Option (A) is incorrect. Timing and graphing measure how many words a student reads correctly in a minute; they do not teach a student where to pause or how to vary pitch. This option reflects the common misconception that rate is the whole of fluency, so raising speed is assumed to produce expression.
distractor_explanations.Having students practice reading lists o: Assuming word-level decoding practice transfers on its own to expressive reading of connected text Option (C) is incorrect. Reading word lists that follow a pattern builds accuracy with specific spellings, but the words are read one at a time with no phrase boundaries to observe. This option reflects the common misconception that word-level decoding practice transfers on its own to expressive reading of connected text.

subject: Teaching Reading
stimulus: After the flood, the basement was uninhabitable.
stem: A fourth-grade teacher asks students to determine the literal meaning of "uninhabitable" in the sentence above. Which teacher move best combines syntactic and morphological analysis?
choices: Asking students what part of speech the word is in the sentence, then what the base "inhabit" and the suffix "-able" contribute to its meaning
Asking students to reread the sentence and tell how they think the family felt about the basement
Asking students to list other words they know that begin with the letters "un"
Asking students to substitute a familiar word and check whether the sentence still makes sense
correct_answer: Asking students what part of speech the word is in the sentence, then what the base "inhabit" and the suffix "-able" contribute to its meaning
explanation: The question requires an understanding of how syntax and morphology work together to establish a word's literal meaning. Recognizing the word as a predicate adjective tells students that it describes the basement, and analyzing un- + inhabit + -able shows that the word means "not able to be lived in." The two sources of information converge on the same literal meaning instead of leaving students with a vague impression.

distractor_explanations.Asking students to reread the sentence a: Treating the inference of feeling or tone as the same task as determining a word's literal meaning Option (B) is incorrect. Asking how the family felt directs students toward tone, connotation, or inference about characters, none of which is the literal meaning of the word. This option reflects the common misconception that inferring a feeling from a text is the same task as determining what an unfamiliar word denotes.
distractor_explanations.Asking students to list other words they: Treating recognition of a familiar affix as complete morphological analysis Option (C) is incorrect. Listing other words that begin with the same letters draws attention to one prefix while leaving the base word and the suffix unexamined, and it never connects the word to its role in the sentence. This option reflects the common misconception that spotting a familiar affix counts as complete morphological analysis.
distractor_explanations.Asking students to substitute a familiar: Assuming that a substitution which still sounds right proves the literal meaning has been established Option (D) is incorrect. Substituting a familiar word can approximate meaning when the surrounding text supplies strong clues, but it bypasses the structural analysis that lets students work out words in sparse contexts, and a substitution that merely sounds plausible is not evidence of the literal meaning. This option reflects the common misconception that a sentence that still sounds right proves the meaning has been established.

subject: Teaching Reading
stem: A reading specialist is designing fluency instruction for a second grader who reads accurately but laboriously. Which set of activities best addresses the skills that support fluent reading at the phoneme, word, and passage levels?
choices: Echo reading of pattern books, choral reading of poems, and partner retelling of stories
Word sorts by onset and rime, weekly spelling tests, and written responses to literature
Vocabulary previews, silent independent reading, and comprehension strategy lessons
Phoneme blending drills, timed practice with high-frequency word lists, and repeated oral reading of short decodable passages
correct_answer: Phoneme blending drills, timed practice with high-frequency word lists, and repeated oral reading of short decodable passages
explanation: The question requires an understanding of how to teach strategies that support fluent reading at each level of text. Phoneme blending makes word recognition efficient enough to support accuracy, timed word-list practice builds the automatic retrieval that raises rate, and repeated reading of connected text lets students integrate those words into phrases. Leaving out any one level means the others are practiced without the support they need.

distractor_explanations.Echo reading of pattern books, choral re: Assuming repeated reading of connected text is sufficient fluency instruction at every level Option (B) is incorrect. Echo reading, choral reading, and retelling are passage-level routines; none of them gives the student systematic work at the phoneme or word level, where word recognition is still effortful. This option reflects the common misconception that reading connected text repeatedly is sufficient fluency instruction at every level.
distractor_explanations.Word sorts by onset and rime, weekly spe: Treating word study routines such as sorting as interchangeable with fluency practice Option (C) is incorrect. Word sorts and spelling tests build orthographic and encoding knowledge, and written responses address comprehension, but none of these asks students to read connected text fluently. This option reflects the common misconception that word study routines such as sorting are interchangeable with fluency practice.
distractor_explanations.Vocabulary previews, silent independent: Assuming that more time with text in any form will produce fluency Option (D) is incorrect. Vocabulary and comprehension instruction support meaning but do not build the automaticity this student lacks, and silent reading gives the teacher no evidence of how the text is actually being read. This option reflects the common misconception that more time with text, in any form, will produce fluency.

subject: Teaching Reading
stem: A fifth-grade teacher notices that many students write long run-on sentences in their science reports. Which instructional approach best uses written language structure to address the problem?
choices: Providing daily sentence-combining practice using mentor sentences taken from the class read-aloud
Assigning grammar worksheets that require students to label parts of speech in isolated sentences
Requiring students to recopy a published paragraph in their best handwriting each morning
Having students memorize the definition of a complete sentence and write it out weekly
correct_answer: Providing daily sentence-combining practice using mentor sentences taken from the class read-aloud
explanation: The question requires an understanding of how to teach written language structure in the context of real writing. Mentor sentences give students models of mature syntax, and combining short sentences into longer ones forces them to decide where one clause ends and the next begins and which mark signals that boundary. The work happens inside meaningful text rather than in isolation, so it transfers to their own writing.

distractor_explanations.Assigning grammar worksheets that requir: Assuming that knowing grammar terminology produces control of syntax in one's own writing Option (B) is incorrect. Labeling parts of speech in sentences someone else wrote is identification practice; it does not require students to make the boundary decisions that produce a run-on in the first place. This option reflects the common misconception that knowing grammar terminology produces control of syntax in one's own writing.
distractor_explanations.Requiring students to recopy a published: Assuming written language conventions are learned through transcription Option (C) is incorrect. Copying text addresses handwriting and attention to printed form, and because the model is already punctuated correctly, it asks students to make no decisions about sentence boundaries. This option reflects the common misconception that written language conventions are learned through transcription.
distractor_explanations.Having students memorize the definition: Treating verbal recall of a rule as the same as applying that rule while composing Option (D) is incorrect. A student can state the definition of a complete sentence and still not apply it while composing, because the difficulty lies in applying the concept under the demands of writing.
