Option (B) is incorrect. Looking words up independently leaves students to choose among multiple senses without guidance, and they frequently pick the first or shortest entry. This option reflects the common misconception that independent dictionary work is an efficient substitute for teacher-directed preteaching. Independence is a long-term goal, but it is not the way to prepare a class for one specific difficult text.

subject: Teaching Reading
stem: Ms. Reed's third graders read the same grade-level passage. Devin reads 104 words correct per minute with smooth phrasing but answers one of five comprehension questions correctly. Marisol reads 61 words correct per minute, stopping often to work out words, and answers four of five correctly. Which interpretation of this pattern is most accurate?
choices: Automatic word recognition is sufficient for comprehension, so Devin's low score must reflect careless answering.
Automatic word recognition frees attention for meaning but does not supply the meaning itself, so comprehension also depends on the knowledge and language a reader brings to the text.
Reading rate determines how much of a text is retained, so Marisol's slower reading should have left her remembering less than Devin.
Comprehension is built almost entirely from background knowledge, so how automatically a student reads has little to do with it.
correct_answer: Automatic word recognition frees attention for meaning but does not supply the meaning itself, so comprehension also depends on the knowledge and language a reader brings to the text.
explanation: The question requires an understanding of how fluency contributes to comprehension. Automatic word recognition takes the word-level bottleneck out of reading so that attention can go to meaning, and that is the whole reason fluency matters. What the freed attention then operates on is the reader's language, vocabulary, and knowledge of the topic. Devin's smooth reading shows the bridge is in place, not that he crossed it, and Marisol's slow but thoughtful reading shows that a reader can construct meaning even while word recognition is still effortful. For instruction the practical point is that fluency is necessary without being sufficient.

distractor_explanations.Automatic word recognition is sufficient: Equating fluent, automatic reading with comprehension, so that a smooth performance is accepted as proof that meaning was constructed. Option (A) is incorrect. Fluent word recognition releases attention for meaning; it does not guarantee that meaning gets built, and a student can read a passage beautifully and take almost nothing from it. This option reflects the common misconception that fluency is sufficient for comprehension. A teacher who holds it will hunt for carelessness or a behavior problem instead of examining Devin's vocabulary and language comprehension, which is where his difficulty actually sits.
distractor_explanations.Reading rate determines how much of a te: Treating reading rate as the cause of retention rather than as a symptom of how automatically the words were recognized. Option (C) is incorrect. Marisol reads more slowly and comprehends more, which is direct evidence against rate as the cause of retention; rate reports how automatically the words were recognized, not how much was understood. This option reflects the common misconception that speed produces comprehension. Acting on it would push Devin to read faster when what he needs is work on the meanings he is not getting from the page.
distractor_explanations.Comprehension is built almost entirely f: Treating background knowledge as the whole of comprehension, so that fluent word recognition is dismissed as unrelated to understanding. Option (D) is incorrect. Background knowledge strongly shapes comprehension, but it operates on meanings the reader still has to get off the page, and a reader who stalls on every other word cannot bring that knowledge to bear. This option reflects the common misconception that one contributor to comprehension makes the others irrelevant. Fluency and vocabulary each remove a different bottleneck, and instruction has to address whichever one is blocking a particular reader.

subject: Teaching Reading
stem: A third grader reads a grade-level passage at 116 words correct per minute with 98 percent accuracy, but in a flat, even voice that runs straight through commas and periods, and he cannot retell what the passage said. Which interpretation of this performance is most accurate?
choices: Accuracy is still too low to support comprehension, so instruction should return to decoding individual words.
The student is fluent, because both rate and accuracy are at or above the benchmark for the grade.
Word recognition is automatic but the phrasing that groups words into meaning is missing, so the reading sounds smooth while producing little comprehension.
The student read too fast to take in the meaning, and asking him to slow down would restore his comprehension.
correct_answer: Word recognition is automatic but the phrasing that groups words into meaning is missing, so the reading sounds smooth while producing little comprehension.
explanation: The question requires an understanding of what each component of oral reading fluency contributes. Rate and accuracy report that word recognition has become automatic; prosody is the component that shows whether the reader is grouping words into meaningful units, and its absence here is what leaves the student with nothing to retell. Instruction therefore has to give him a phrased model to imitate on text he can already read accurately, rather than more practice on the two components that are already in place.

distractor_explanations.Accuracy is still too low to support com: Attributing any comprehension failure to weak decoding, even when accuracy shows that word recognition is already secure. Option (D) is incorrect. At 98 percent accuracy the student is reading the words that are on the page, so decoding is not what is holding his comprehension back. This option reflects the common misconception that every comprehension failure traces back to weak word recognition. Returning to decoding would reteach a skill this student has already demonstrated and would leave the missing component untouched.
distractor_explanations.The student is fluent, because both rate: Equating fluency with its two countable indicators, so that prosody drops out of the construct entirely. Option (A) is incorrect. Rate and accuracy are the two components that are easiest to count, but fluency also includes prosody, and this student's reading shows exactly what is missing when that component is left out. This option reflects the common misconception that fluency is fully described by a words-correct-per-minute score. Benchmarks screen for risk; they do not establish that the reader is building meaning.
distractor_explanations.The student read too fast to take in the: Assuming that slowing the reading down will produce comprehension, when rate is not what is keeping the reader from the meaning. Option (C) is incorrect. Rate is not the problem here: reading the same flat phrasing more slowly would produce the same empty result, because slowing down does not group words into meaningful units. This option reflects the common misconception that rate is the lever to pull whenever comprehension fails. What has to change is phrasing, and phrasing is taught through a model and rereading, not through pacing.

subject: Teaching Reading
stem: Ms. Alvarez's third graders stop at the sentence "The arid desert received almost no rain all year." She wants to show them how to work out the meaning of "arid" by combining context, syntax, and word-structure knowledge. Which teacher move best models that process?
choices: Having the students sound out arid syllable by syllable before rereading the sentence
Having the students skip the word, finish the sentence, and put in a word that sounds right
Telling the students that arid means "dry" and having them write the definition three times
Asking what the sentence says happens to the desert, what part of speech arid must be, and whether any word parts look familiar, then checking the candidate meaning against the sentence
correct_answer: Asking what the sentence says happens to the desert, what part of speech arid must be, and whether any word parts look familiar, then checking the candidate meaning against the sentence
explanation: The question requires an understanding of how systematic and explicit instruction is delivered for word-solving. By asking what the sentence reports, what part of speech the word must be, and whether any word parts are familiar, the teacher models a routine that draws on context, syntax, and morphology together and then verifies the candidate meaning against the sentence. The questioning makes the thinking visible, so students can run the same routine on the next unfamiliar word without her.

distractor_explanations.Having the students sound out arid sylla: Treating successful decoding as if it yielded meaning, when it yields only pronunciation. Option (C) is incorrect. Sounding out arid helps students pronounce the word, but pronunciation does not deliver meaning. This option reflects the common misconception that decoding a word and understanding it are a single achievement. Students who can read a word aloud accurately may still have no idea what it means.
distractor_explanations.Having the students skip the word, finis: Treating an unverified plausible substitution as equivalent to a checked inference from context and word structure. Option (D) is incorrect. Substituting a word that sounds right may produce a plausible reading, but plausibility is not evidence, and students have no way to tell whether their guess matches the author's meaning. This option reflects the common misconception that any context-based guess counts as strategic word learning. Without checking the guess against context, syntax, and word parts, the strategy is unreliable.
distractor_explanations.Telling the students that arid means \"d: Confusing the delivery of an answer with the teaching of a procedure, so that explicit instruction is reduced to telling. Option (A) is incorrect. Supplying the definition ends the reasoning before it begins and leaves students with nothing to use on the next unfamiliar word. This option reflects the common misconception that telling a word's meaning is teaching a strategy. A definition is a product; the transferable thing is the procedure for arriving at it.

subject: Teaching Reading
stem: A third-grade teacher is deciding whether a student's fluency problem should be addressed at the phoneme level, the word level, or the passage level. The student reads a grade-level passage accurately but in short bursts, and the stops come almost entirely on words of two or three syllables. Given a list of one-syllable high-frequency words, the student reads quickly and without hesitation. Which instructional decision is best supported by this evidence?
choices: Work at the word level on common syllable patterns and word parts, because the stops inside longer words are what break the student's reading into fragments.
Work at the passage level on phrasing and expression, because the student already reads accurately and mainly needs a model to imitate.
Increase the amount of timed repeated reading, because raising rate will eventually pull the slower recognition of longer words along with it.
Start at the phoneme level with blending and segmenting, because slow oral reading shows that phonemic awareness is still weak.
correct_answer: Work at the word level on common syllable patterns and word parts, because the stops inside longer words are what break the student's reading into fragments.
explanation: The question requires an understanding of how instruction is matched to the level at which reading breaks down. The student already retrieves one-syllable high-frequency words in one step, so the breakdown sits inside longer words, and teaching common syllable patterns and frequent word parts is what makes those words retrievable the same way. Once the longer words come automatically the stops disappear, and phrasing finally has continuous text to work on, which is why the word level is the right place to start.

distractor_explanations.Work at the passage level on phrasing an: Reading accuracy as automaticity, so that passage-level phrasing work is prescribed while recognition of individual words is still effortful. Option (C) is incorrect. The accuracy here is accuracy bought one word at a time, and phrasing cannot be layered over reading that keeps stopping inside words. This option reflects the common misconception that accurate reading is the same as automatic reading. A model of phrased reading is valuable once the words can be retrieved without effort, and pushing it earlier just gives the student a target he cannot reach.
distractor_explanations.Increase the amount of timed repeated re: Applying timed repeated reading as a universal fluency remedy, without first identifying which level is causing the breakdown. Option (D) is incorrect. Repeated reading is a sound passage-level routine, but timing the student over words he must still work out practices the stop-and-start pattern instead of removing its cause. This option reflects the common misconception that a favored fluency routine applies at every level of the problem. Matching the routine to the level where reading actually breaks down is what makes the practice pay off.
distractor_explanations.Start at the phoneme level with blending: Tracing slow oral reading to a phonemic awareness deficit even when the student decodes accurately, and defaulting to the lowest level of instruction. Option (A) is incorrect. The student reads the words accurately, which means the sounds are being blended successfully; phonemic awareness work would treat a difficulty this student does not have. This option reflects the common misconception that any slow oral reading points back to a phonemic awareness deficit. Reaching for the lowest level of the hierarchy spends instructional time that this student needs at the word level.

subject: Teaching Reading
stem: A second-grade teacher notices that many students leave out capitalization and end punctuation in their own writing even though they complete workbook pages on those rules correctly. Which instructional change best addresses the gap?
choices: Assigning additional workbook pages on capitalization and punctuation for homework each night
Having students revise sentences taken from their own writing using a class editing checklist
Having students copy a published paragraph to practice neat handwriting
Reviewing the capitalization and punctuation rules on the board before each writing period
correct_answer: Having students revise sentences taken from their own writing using a class editing checklist
explanation: The question requires an understanding of how the conventions of written language are taught. Revising a sentence from their own writing, using a checklist the class has built, asks students to make an editing decision in a meaningful context instead of recalling a rule in isolation. Because the sentence is theirs, the correction is tied to a real communicative purpose, and that connection is what carries over into later writing.

distractor_explanations.Assigning additional workbook pages on c: Attributing a failure to apply knowledge to insufficient practice quantity, rather than to a mismatch between practice format and application context. Option (A) is incorrect. More workbook pages supply more practice in the very format that has already failed to transfer. This option reflects the common misconception that a transfer problem is a practice-volume problem. Students who can complete the pages but not apply the conventions in their own writing need a different kind of task, not more of the same one.
distractor_explanations.Having students copy a published paragra: Confusing the conventions of written language with neat handwriting, so that correct-looking transcription is mistaken for editing competence. Option (C) is incorrect. Copying a model gives students correct forms to look at but requires no decision from them, so nothing changes in their own writing. This option reflects the common misconception that conventions are a handwriting or transcription skill. Conventions involve editing choices, and copying removes the need to make any.
distractor_explanations.Reviewing the capitalization and punctua: Assuming that stating a rule again will produce the ability to use it, when the missing piece is guided application. Option (D) is incorrect. Restating the rules adds nothing for students who already know them well enough to pass the workbook pages. This option reflects the common misconception that knowing a rule is the same as applying it while composing. The gap here is application, and application is built through guided practice in editing real sentences.

subject: Teaching Reading
stem: To encourage independent word learning, a fourth-grade teacher has students keep personal word-collection notebooks during independent reading. Which additional step most strengthens the practice?
choices: Requiring students to collect a set number of words each week
Having students copy the dictionary entry for each word they collect
Building in regular sharing and discussion so collected words get further encounters in new contexts
Quizzing students every Friday on the words in their notebooks
correct_answer: Building in regular sharing and discussion so collected words get further encounters in new contexts
explanation: The question requires an understanding of how direct instruction and independent learning work together in vocabulary development. Independent collection gives students ownership of the words, but words are learned through repeated and varied encounters, and scheduled sharing and discussion supply those encounters. It also gives the teacher a chance to correct meanings students have guessed wrong, which is what turns a private list into durable knowledge.

distractor_explanations.Requiring students to collect a set numb: Measuring vocabulary learning by the quantity of words collected rather than by the quality of the encounters with each one. Option (A) is incorrect. A weekly quota pushes students to fill pages with easy or incidental words instead of noticing the words they actually need. This option reflects the common misconception that the number of words gathered determines how much is learned. Depth of processing matters more than the count of entries.
distractor_explanations.Having students copy the dictionary entr: Equating recording a word in a notebook with acquiring its meaning, treating the notebook as the product rather than as a prompt for later encounters. Option (B) is incorrect. Copying a dictionary entry is transcription, and entries typically list several senses without indicating which one fits the student's text. This option reflects the common misconception that recording a definition is equivalent to learning a word. Writing words down does not produce the multiple meaningful encounters that word learning requires.
distractor_explanations.Quizzing students every Friday on the wo: Treating testing as a substitute for instruction, as though measuring retention would produce the learning being measured. Option (D) is incorrect. A weekly quiz measures what students remember but does nothing to create the encounters through which they would learn the words in the first place. This option reflects the common misconception that testing can substitute for teaching. Assessment reports on learning; it does not generate it.

subject: Teaching Reading
stem: Which practice most effectively builds students' academic and domain-specific vocabulary over the course of a unit?
choices: Posting the unit's words on a word wall at the start of the unit
Having students look up unfamiliar words on their own as they meet them while reading
Introducing each target word once, with a clear definition, before students read
Providing multiple encounters with each target word across speaking, listening, reading, and writing
correct_answer: Providing multiple encounters with each target word across speaking, listening, reading, and writing
explanation: The question requires an understanding of how vocabulary knowledge is built and why it matters for comprehension. Word knowledge deepens across encounters, and moving a word through talk, listening, reading, and writing forces students to meet it in different contexts and to use it actively rather than merely recognize it. That is what turns a word a student has heard into a word the student can read and think with, which is what comprehension runs on.

distractor_explanations.Posting the unit's words on a word wall: Confusing the display of words with the teaching of words, treating visibility as if it produced processing. Option (C) is incorrect. A word wall displays the words and reminds students of them, but display alone does not require anyone to process meaning. This option reflects the common misconception that making words visible is the same as teaching them. Environmental print supports instruction that is already happening; it does not deliver that instruction.
distractor_explanations.Having students look up unfamiliar words: Assuming that vocabulary is acquired incidentally through wide reading, so that direct instruction of academic and domain-specific words is unnecessary. Option (D) is incorrect. Left on their own, students often skip unfamiliar words, choose the wrong sense from a dictionary, or give up on the text. This option reflects the common misconception that wide reading by itself builds the academic vocabulary students need. Incidental learning from context is slow and unreliable, and it is least reliable for the students who start with the smallest vocabularies.
distractor_explanations.Introducing each target word once, with: Treating preteaching as a one-time event of giving a definition, when one exposure cannot build durable word knowledge. Option (A) is incorrect. A single clear introduction is a useful beginning, but one exposure rarely produces a word a student can access while reading independently. This option reflects the common misconception that preteaching vocabulary consists of defining a word once. Preteaching opens a word's instructional life; it does not complete it.

subject: Teaching Reading
stem: A first grader reads a familiar passage quickly but often substitutes words that fit the meaning, such as reading "house" for "home." Which instructional response best addresses this pattern?
choices: Teaching the student to check whether the word read matches the letters on the page before moving on
Moving the student to a harder text so that more challenging words build vocabulary
Having the student work on expression, since the substitutions show that meaning is being monitored
Encouraging the student to read a little faster so that the substitutions disrupt the meaning less
correct_answer: Teaching the student to check whether the word read matches the letters on the page before moving on
explanation: The question requires an understanding of how accuracy is taught within oral reading fluency. Substitutions that make sense show that the student is predicting from meaning rather than working through the print, so the remedy is to make the print the check: the student compares what was said against the letters and self-corrects. Teaching that checking routine builds accurate word recognition, which has to be in place before rate or expression can be worked on productively.

distractor_explanations.Moving the student to a harder text so t: Attributing meaningful substitutions to a vocabulary gap and responding with harder text, which increases the guessing the teacher wants to reduce. Option (C) is incorrect. Harder text multiplies the number of words the student does not know and therefore the number of guesses the student will make. This option reflects the common misconception that substitutions come from a vocabulary gap and should be answered with more advanced text. The difficulty here is checking the print, and adding difficulty will not teach that skill.
distractor_explanations.Having the student work on expression, s: Reading meaningful substitutions as evidence of comprehension to be praised, rather than as evidence of inattention to print. Option (D) is incorrect. Expression work is appropriate once the student is reading the words that are actually on the page; practicing prosody on substituted text builds fluency over the wrong words. This option reflects the common misconception that meaningful substitutions are a sign of comprehension to be encouraged. They are a sign that the student is not attending closely to print.
distractor_explanations.Encouraging the student to read a little: Treating rate as the primary target of fluency instruction and pushing speed before the student reads the words accurately. Option (A) is incorrect. More speed leaves the student less time to look at the letters and typically produces more guessing, not less. This option reflects the common misconception that fluency means reading quickly and that rate should be pushed first. Accuracy is the foundation of fluency, and pushing rate before accuracy entrenches the guessing habit.

subject: Teaching Reading
stem: A fourth grader reads the sentence "The scientist's hypothesis was not supported, so she revised it." Asked what hypothesis means, the student says, "It's what you think will happen before you test it, because she had to change it after the test." Which best describes the strategy the student used?
choices: Morphological analysis, because the student broke the word into its Greek roots
Context and syntax, because the student used the sentence's cause-and-effect structure to infer a meaning
Prior knowledge, because the student already knew about experiments and ignored the text
Substitution, because the student put in a word that sounded right without checking it
correct_answer: Context and syntax, because the student used the sentence's cause-and-effect structure to infer a meaning
explanation: The question requires an understanding of how readers infer the meanings of unfamiliar words. The student reads the cause-and-effect relation across the two clauses, notices that the hypothesis was revised after the test, and concludes that it must be the idea formed beforehand. The explanation cites evidence from the sentence, which is what distinguishes a strategic inference from a guess.

distractor_explanations.Morphological analysis, because the stud: Assuming that any correct inference about an academic word came from analyzing its word parts, regardless of the evidence the student actually cited. Option (A) is incorrect. The student's explanation never refers to word parts, roots, or affixes, so morphology took no part in the reasoning. This option reflects the common misconception that a successful inference about an academic word must have been morphological. Words of Greek or Latin origin invite that assumption, but the evidence this student used came from the sentence.
distractor_explanations.Prior knowledge, because the student alr: Attributing a text-based inference to background knowledge whenever the topic is familiar, which hides the strategy the student actually used. Option (C) is incorrect. The student explicitly grounds the inference in the sentence rather than in outside knowledge, pointing to what had to be revised after the test. This option reflects the common misconception that a sensible inference about a familiar topic must have come from background knowledge. Attributing it to prior knowledge would tell the teacher that no strategy instruction is needed, which the evidence does not support.
distractor_explanations.Substitution, because the student put in: Dismissing every context-based inference as an unverified guess, and missing the difference between substituting and checking. Option (D) is incorrect. A substitution becomes a guess only when the reader does not check it, and this student supplies a reason tied to the text and produces a meaning consistent with it. This option reflects the common misconception that any inference is merely a plausible substitution. Checking the candidate meaning against the surrounding text is exactly what makes the strategy work.

subject: Teaching Reading
stem: A fourth-grade teacher writes these sentences on the board: "The wind blew." "The wind was cold." "The wind rattled the windows." She asks students to combine them into a single sentence. What does this activity primarily develop?
choices: Students' ability to read aloud with appropriate expression
Students' ability to decode unfamiliar multisyllabic words
Students' understanding of how sentence structure can be manipulated to combine ideas
Students' knowledge of irregular plural spellings
correct_answer: Students' understanding of how sentence structure can be manipulated to combine ideas
explanation: The question requires an understanding of how the structure of written language is taught. To combine the sentences, students must decide which idea becomes the main clause, which are reduced to modifiers, and what punctuation joins them, so the task puts syntax into their hands rather than in front of them as a rule to memorize. Because the meaning is already built, they can concentrate on the structural choices.

distractor_explanations.Students' ability to read aloud with app: Labeling any activity involving sentences as fluency practice, when the task asks students to construct structure rather than to perform it. Option (D) is incorrect. Students may eventually read their combined sentences aloud more smoothly, but expression is a by-product rather than the object of the lesson. This option reflects the common misconception that any sentence-level activity counts as fluency practice. The work students do here is on constructing structure, not on performing it.
distractor_explanations.Students' ability to decode unfamiliar m: Treating any sentence-level task as decoding practice, and missing that the work here is on structure rather than on sounding out words. Option (A) is incorrect. All three sentences are made of words the students can already read, so no decoding is required. This option reflects the common misconception that any work with printed sentences is decoding work. The activity operates on how words are arranged, not on how individual words are sounded out.
distractor_explanations.Students' knowledge of irregular plural: Reducing written language structure to spelling and conventions, so that syntactic work is overlooked entirely. Option (C) is incorrect. Plural spellings are incidental here, and none of the sentences turns on them. This option reflects the common misconception that instruction in written language is mainly a matter of spelling and other conventions. Conventions are one part of written structure, but this task is about how clauses are built and joined.

subject: Teaching Reading
stem: Several third graders who are multilingual learners use words such as "harbor" and "current" correctly when they talk about their own neighborhoods, but they do not select those words correctly on a standardized vocabulary check. What is the most reasonable interpretation of this pattern?
choices: The students are guessing, because conversational use is not evidence of word knowledge.
The check is invalid and should be removed from the students' records.
The students have a vocabulary deficit that requires intensive remediation.
The check may not be capturing knowledge the students demonstrate in other settings, so the teacher should gather additional evidence.
correct_answer: The check may not be capturing knowledge the students demonstrate in other settings, so the teacher should gather additional evidence.
explanation: The question requires an understanding of how assessment information is interpreted for students whose experiences differ. Correct use in conversation is genuine evidence of word knowledge, so when one measure disagrees with it, the reasonable reading is that the measure samples a narrower slice of what the students know. Gathering further evidence through observation, discussion, and classroom tasks before drawing conclusions is what keeps a single score from being mistaken for the whole picture.

distractor_explanations.The students are guessing, because conve: Treating only decontextualized test performance as valid evidence, and rejecting appropriate spontaneous use as mere guessing. Option (C) is incorrect. Using a word appropriately in spontaneous speech about a familiar topic is among the strongest available evidence of word knowledge. This option reflects the common misconception that only decontextualized test performance counts as knowing a word. Dismissing the conversational evidence would discard the most informative data the teacher has.
distractor_explanations.The check is invalid and should be remov: Jumping from "this one measure looks wrong here" to "the measure is invalid," when the right response is to add evidence rather than delete it. Option (D) is incorrect. A measure can be limited for one purpose without being worthless; the check may still contribute useful information when combined with other sources. This option reflects the common misconception that a measure showing a discrepancy must be entirely invalid. The appropriate response is to triangulate with further evidence, not to discard a data source.
distractor_explanations.The students have a vocabulary deficit t: Treating a low score on a single measure as proof of a deficit within the student, regardless of contradicting evidence from other settings. Option (A) is incorrect. Calling this a deficit would require evidence that the students lack the words, and their spontaneous conversational use is evidence against it. This option reflects the common misconception that a low score on one measure settles the question of what a student knows. Reading a difference in performance across settings as a deficit inside the student is exactly the error to avoid.

subject: Teaching Reading
stem: A second-grade teacher reviews running records and finds that several students decode single-syllable short-vowel words accurately but consistently misread longer words such as "boat," "tree," and "play." Which spelling pattern should the teacher introduce first with these students?
choices: Vowel teams, such as the vowel pair in "boat"
R-controlled vowels, such as the vowel sound in "car"
Closed syllables, such as the vowel sound in "cat"
Consonant clusters, such as the /st/ at the beginning of "stop"
correct_answer: Vowel teams, such as the vowel pair in "boat"
explanation: The question requires an understanding of instructional strategies for common phonics patterns. The words the students are missing all contain two vowels that work together to represent one sound. Introducing vowel teams directly targets the pattern appearing in the students' errors, which is the most efficient use of instructional time.

distractor_explanations.R-controlled vowels, such as the vowel s: Equating a high-frequency phonics pattern with the pattern that deserves priority. Relevance to the misreadings is what makes a pattern worth teaching now. R-controlled vowels are a legitimate phonics pattern, but they do not appear in the words the students are misreading. Teaching it now would address a pattern that is not yet causing difficulty while leaving the actual gap unaddressed.
distractor_explanations.Closed syllables, such as the vowel soun: Treating what students already read correctly as what they need to be taught. Re-teaching a secure pattern adds no new decoding power. Closed syllables with short vowels are exactly what these students already read accurately. Re-teaching a mastered pattern adds no new decoding power and does not address the multi-vowel patterns in the error words.
distractor_explanations.Consonant clusters, such as the /st/ at: Confusing a pattern students have already mastered with the pattern generating their errors. The error data, not the scope and sequence, should set the teaching point. Students who decode single-syllable words accurately are generally already handling initial consonant clusters successfully. This instruction would target a pattern the students have essentially mastered rather than the one producing their errors.

subject: Teaching Reading
stem: A fourth-grade student reads the word "unhappy" accurately. When asked what it means, the student says, "It means you are happy again — the 'un' part makes it happen two times." Which analysis of this response is most accurate?
choices: The student has confused the prefix un- with the prefix re-.
The student has correctly identified the base word but has not yet learned any prefixes.
The student has applied a closed-syllable decoding strategy to a multisyllabic word.
The student has confused the suffix -y with the prefix un-.
correct_answer: The student has confused the prefix un- with the prefix re-.
explanation: The question requires an understanding of how to analyze student responses to identify partial conceptions. The student correctly identifies "happy" as the base and correctly recognizes that the added letters form an affix, but assigns the wrong meaning to it. The meaning given, "happen two times" or "again," is the meaning of re-, not un-. This is a partial conception: the structural analysis is sound while the semantic assignment is not.

distractor_explanations.The student has correctly identified the: Mistaking a partial conception for the complete absence of one. Because the structural analysis is sound, instruction should refine the idea rather than start over. This analysis understates what the student demonstrated. The student did apply prefix knowledge by attributing a specific meaning to un-, which means instruction should refine an existing concept rather than introduce prefixes from scratch.
distractor_explanations.The student has applied a closed-syllabl: Confusing a decoding difficulty with a meaning difficulty. Accurate oral reading rules out syllabication as the obstacle and points to morphological meaning instead. The student read the word accurately, so decoding is not the difficulty. The error appears only when the student explains the meaning, which places the problem at the level of morphological meaning rather than syllable-based word attack.
distractor_explanations.The student has confused the suffix -y w: Misjudging where the affix boundary falls by taking a letter inside the base as the affix under discussion. The student's explicit reference to un- is the decisive evidence. The student's comment focuses entirely on "un" and attributes a meaning to it. The final -y in "happy" belongs to the base word and plays no part in the student's explanation, so the confusion is between two prefixes, not between a prefix and a suffix.

subject: Teaching Reading
stem: A teacher is planning instruction for students who decode closed-syllable words such as "cat" and "mop" accurately but stumble on "baking" and "theme." Which syllable type should the teacher introduce next?
choices: Closed syllables
Vowel-consonant-e (VCe) syllables
R-controlled syllables
Open syllables
correct_answer: Vowel-consonant-e (VCe) syllables
explanation: The question requires an understanding of syllable types and the sequence in which they are taught. Both 'baking' and 'theme' follow a long-vowel, single-consonant, silent-e pattern, so teaching the VCe pattern explains why the final e is silent while the preceding vowel says its long sound.

distractor_explanations.Closed syllables: Recommending instruction in a skill the student has already mastered. The prompt explicitly rules this out by describing what students can already do. A closed syllable ends in a consonant and its vowel is short. The prompt states that students already read closed-syllable words accurately, so reteaching this type does not address the observed difficulty.
distractor_explanations.R-controlled syllables: Broadening 'a vowel followed by a consonant' into a single category. Which consonant follows the vowel determines the syllable type. R-controlled syllables are those in which a vowel is followed by r, as in 'car' or 'bird.' In 'baking' and 'theme' the long vowel is followed by k and m respectively, not by r.
distractor_explanations.Open syllables: Inferring that a long vowel always signals an open syllable. A long vowel can also arise from a VCe pattern or a vowel team. An open syllable ends in a vowel and that vowel is long, as in the first syllable of 'ta-ble.' In these words the vowel is followed by a consonant, so the pattern does not apply.

subject: Teaching Reading
stem: A teacher wants students to be able to determine the meaning of unfamiliar multimorphemic words such as "unhappiness." Which instructional approach best supports that goal?
choices: Having students locate the word in a dictionary and copy the entry into a notebook
Having students sound out the word syllable by syllable and check their pronunciation against a picture
Guiding students to identify the prefix, base word, and suffix and then combine their meanings
Providing the definition and asking students to use the word in a written sentence
correct_answer: Guiding students to identify the prefix, base word, and suffix and then combine their meanings
explanation: The question requires an understanding of morphological analysis as a word-solving strategy. Separating 'un-' (not), 'happy,' and '-ness' (state of) and recombining their meanings gives students a transferable procedure they can apply to new multimorphemic words.

distractor_explanations.Having students locate the word in a dic: Treating access to a reference tool as equivalent to instruction in deriving word meaning. Dictionary lookup is a reference skill rather than an analysis strategy, and copying an entry produces only shallow contact with the word. It also interrupts reading rather than supporting it.
distractor_explanations.Having students sound out the word sylla: Equating successful pronunciation with comprehension of meaning. The Simple View of Reading treats word recognition and language comprehension as distinct contributors. Sounding out a word addresses pronunciation, not meaning. Decoding and comprehension are separate components of reading, and a student can produce a word aloud with no idea what it means.
distractor_explanations.Providing the definition and asking stud: Confusing providing an answer with teaching a strategy. Instruction should build a capability that transfers to untaught words. Supplying a definition gives students the meaning of this one word but teaches no procedure. Confronted later with 'unwillingness,' they are no better equipped than before.

subject: Teaching Reading
stem: A teacher is planning word-analysis instruction and wants the end-of-year target to match grade-level expectations. Which decoding task is most appropriate for students at the end of first grade?
choices: Using morphological analysis to unlock the meaning of words such as "unhappy" and "replay"
Using context to confirm the pronunciation of multisyllabic content words such as "habitat"
Blending three phonemes to read single-syllable words such as "cat" and "mop"
Decoding two-syllable words with common long-vowel patterns such as "paper" and "reptile"
correct_answer: Decoding two-syllable words with common long-vowel patterns such as "paper" and "reptile"
explanation: The question requires an understanding of how word-analysis expectations shift by grade. By the end of first grade, students are expected to apply their letter-sound knowledge to two-syllable words that follow regular patterns, dividing the word into syllables and reading each part before blending them into a known word.

distractor_explanations.Using morphological analysis to unlock t: Introducing morphological analysis before students can reliably decode single- and two-syllable words Morphological analysis of prefixes and suffixes is normally introduced after students reliably decode single- and two-syllable words. Asking first graders to use it as a primary decoding route sets the task well above their current word-analysis repertoire.
distractor_explanations.Using context to confirm the pronunciati: Using context to generate a pronunciation as a substitute for letter-sound analysis Checking a decoded word against context is a useful verification step, but it is not itself a decoding procedure. Using context to generate pronunciation bypasses the letter-sound analysis students need to develop.
distractor_explanations.Blending three phonemes to read single-s: Treating beginning-of-year CVC blending as an appropriate end-of-first-grade decoding target Blending three phonemes in CVC words is an early-first-grade target, not an exit target. Choosing it holds students below grade level and leaves them without the syllable-level strategies the later grades assume.

subject: Teaching Reading
stem: Which statement best describes how high-frequency words such as "said," "was," and "they" should be taught?
choices: By ensuring that students recognize them instantly and automatically through repeated encounters in connected text
By having students sound them out letter by letter each time they appear
By teaching their meanings first so that students can read them with understanding
By grouping them for instruction with other words that share the same spelling pattern
correct_answer: By ensuring that students recognize them instantly and automatically through repeated encounters in connected text
explanation: The question requires an understanding of the purpose of high-frequency word instruction. These words make up a large share of early texts, so the goal is instant recognition; repeated encounters in sentences and books build the automaticity that frees attention for comprehension.

distractor_explanations.By having students sound them out letter: Assuming every high-frequency word should be sounded out, including those with irregular spellings Several of the most frequent English words are spelling outliers: the ai in "said" represents a short e sound, and the ey in "they" is not the expected pattern. Requiring students to blend them every time prevents the automatic recognition the words demand.
distractor_explanations.By teaching their meanings first so that: Confusing oral word meaning with printed word recognition Students almost always know these words orally before they meet them in print. The instructional problem is mapping a familiar spoken word onto an unfamiliar printed form, not teaching a new meaning.
distractor_explanations.By grouping them for instruction with ot: Applying phonics-pattern grouping logic to words selected for their frequency rather than their regularity Pattern-based grouping is the organizing logic of phonics instruction, not of high-frequency word instruction. These words are selected and taught because of how often they occur, not because they illustrate a spelling generalization.

subject: Teaching Reading
stem: A kindergarten teacher writes "was" on the board, says the word, has students repeat it, and then has each student trace the letters in a tray of sand while saying the sounds. This routine primarily supports sight word recognition through
choices: explicit instruction in the meaning of the word
systematic practice in segmenting the word into individual phonemes
repeated, multisensory exposure that links the printed form, the pronunciation, and the physical movement together
practice in using the word in a spoken sentence
correct_answer: repeated, multisensory exposure that links the printed form, the pronunciation, and the physical movement together
explanation: The question requires an understanding of techniques that expand sight word recognition. The routine combines seeing the word, hearing and saying it, and forming the letters by hand, so several sensory pathways are activated for the same spelling at the same time, which strengthens retention and speeds later recognition.

distractor_explanations.explicit instruction in the meaning of t: Mistaking vocabulary instruction for the orthographic mapping that sight word work requires Nothing in the routine addresses what "was" means; students in kindergarten use the word in speech already. The routine targets the printed form, not the definition.
distractor_explanations.systematic practice in segmenting the wo: Equating phonemic segmentation practice with practice in recognizing printed words Segmenting into phonemes is an auditory phonemic awareness task, and it typically stops short of print. This routine keeps the written word in view throughout and asks students to form letters, so the emphasis is on orthographic mapping rather than on sound segmentation alone.
distractor_explanations.practice in using the word in a spoken s: Treating oral sentence production as a route to printed word recognition Producing a spoken sentence exercises oral language and syntax. It gives students no concentrated look at the spelling, which is where the recognition problem lies.

subject: Teaching Reading
stem: A first-grade student writes "kik" for "kick." The teacher notes that every letter the student used represents a plausible sound. Which response best builds the student's understanding of spelling conventions?
choices: Having the student practice forming the letters k, i, and c correctly
Telling the student the correct spelling and having the student copy it five times
Deferring any discussion of the spelling until the student reads more fluently
Explaining that the /k/ sound at the end of a one-syllable word after a short vowel is usually spelled ck, and having the student sort words by their final /k/ spelling
correct_answer: Explaining that the /k/ sound at the end of a one-syllable word after a short vowel is usually spelled ck, and having the student sort words by their final /k/ spelling
explanation: The question requires an understanding of how conventional spellings are taught. The student's attempt is phonetically defensible, so the next move is to make the convention explicit and give the student a set of examples that reveals when the language uses k and when it uses ck. Sorting turns a one-off correction into a generalizable pattern.

distractor_explanations.Having the student practice forming the: Attributing a spelling error to letter formation rather than to an unlearned spelling convention The student's letters are legible and correctly formed; the issue is which letter represents the final sound, not how the letters are written. Handwriting practice would leave the actual error untouched.
distractor_explanations.Telling the student the correct spelling: Equating repeated copying of a corrected word with instruction in a spelling generalization Copying a correct model may fix this one word for this one day, but it does not tell the student why ck is used here. Without attention to the pattern, the same error reappears with "back," "pick," and "duck."
distractor_explanations.Deferring any discussion of the spelling: Assuming instruction in spelling conventions should wait until fluency improves Encoding and decoding develop together, and instruction in one supports the other. Waiting for fluency to improve first delays the spelling knowledge that would support both.

subject: Teaching Reading
stem: A first-grade teacher wants to track students' decoding growth from week to week. Which assessment approach best serves that purpose?
choices: An end-of-unit written test in which students state phonics rules
A brief timed measure in which students read lists of decodable nonsense words
A running record of connected text administered at the end of each grading period
A letter-name inventory administered once in the fall
correct_answer: A brief timed measure in which students read lists of decodable nonsense words
explanation: The question requires an understanding of progress monitoring in foundational skills. A short nonsense word measure is quick enough to repeat frequently, produces a comparable score each time, and forces students to apply letter-sound correspondences rather than retrieve memorized words, which makes it sensitive to decoding growth over short intervals.

distractor_explanations.An end-of-unit written test in which stu: Treating the ability to state a phonics rule as evidence of the ability to apply it while reading Being able to state a rule and being able to apply it while reading are different competencies. A student may recite a generalization accurately and still not use it to read an unfamiliar word.
distractor_explanations.A running record of connected text admin: Using a periodic diagnostic assessment as a progress-monitoring measure A running record gives rich diagnostic detail, but administering it only at the end of a grading period is far too infrequent to show week-to-week movement or to prompt a timely change in instruction.
distractor_explanations.A letter-name inventory administered onc: Confusing screening, which identifies risk, with progress monitoring, which measures response to instruction A once-a-year letter-name inventory is a screening tool used to flag risk. It cannot show whether instruction is working, because it is not repeated and it measures a skill that decoding instruction has already moved past.

subject: Teaching Reading
stem: A first-grade teacher is introducing the r-controlled vowel pattern found in "car," "fork," and "her." Which instructional sequence best reflects research on teaching phonics patterns?
choices: Having students memorize a statement of the rule before they read any words that contain it
Having students read a leveled text first and infer the pattern from the words they meet in it
Having students read words with the pattern, sort those words by the vowel-plus-r spelling, and then read them again in connected decodable text
Having students copy the pattern words and draw a picture to illustrate each meaning
correct_answer: Having students read words with the pattern, sort those words by the vowel-plus-r spelling, and then read them again in connected decodable text
explanation: The question requires an understanding of instructional strategies for common phonics patterns. The sequence is explicit and systematic: students meet the pattern in words, compare examples to see what is regular about it, and then apply it while reading connected text, which is where the pattern has to work automatically.

distractor_explanations.Having students memorize a statement of: Teaching a rule as a statement to be memorized before students have examined any examples A rule stated in the abstract before students have handled any examples is difficult to hold onto and harder still to apply while reading. Patterns are best built from examples students have already read successfully.
distractor_explanations.Having students read a leveled text firs: Assuming incidental contact with words in text is enough for students to infer a phonics pattern Asking beginning readers to infer a pattern from continuous text assumes they will notice the regularity on their own while also managing everything else reading requires. Incidental contact is far less reliable than explicit attention to the pattern.
distractor_explanations.Having students copy the pattern words a: Using copying and illustrating as phonics practice when the attention stays on handwriting and meaning Copying and illustrating keeps students busy with handwriting and meaning while leaving the letter-sound relationship unexamined. The objective is the spelling-to-sound mapping, and this routine never puts attention on it.

subject: Teaching Reading
stem: A second-grade teacher is demonstrating how to read the word "cupcake" by thinking aloud about syllable types. Which explanation best applies that knowledge?
choices: "The first part ends in a consonant, so that vowel is likely short; the second part has a vowel-consonant-e pattern, so that vowel is likely long. I'll try cup-cake."
"Both parts end in a consonant, so both vowels are short. I'll say cup-cak."
"I'll say the sound for each letter and push them together."
"Both parts have two vowels together, so I'll use the long sound in each one."
correct_answer: "The first part ends in a consonant, so that vowel is likely short; the second part has a vowel-consonant-e pattern, so that vowel is likely long. I'll try cup-cake."
explanation: The question requires an understanding of how syllable-type knowledge is explained to students. The teacher names the two different syllable types in the word, states the vowel expectation each one carries, and then uses those expectations to generate a pronunciation, which is exactly the reasoning students need to hear modeled before they can do it themselves.

distractor_explanations.\"Both parts end in a consonant, so both: Applying the closed-syllable expectation to a vowel-consonant-e syllable The second syllable is not closed; it ends in a vowel-consonant-e pattern, so applying the closed-syllable expectation to it produces a nonword. This explanation overgeneralizes one syllable type across a word that contains two different ones.
distractor_explanations.\"I'll say the sound for each letter and: Substituting letter-by-letter blending for the syllable-level analysis longer words require Saying each letter sound and blending may work for short single-syllable words, but it gives students nothing to use on longer words. A demonstration of syllable types should show the larger unit of analysis, not retreat to letter-by-letter blending.
distractor_explanations.\"Both parts have two vowels together, s: Misreading a syllable's internal structure and treating it as a vowel team Neither syllable contains a vowel team. Describing the word this way misreads its structure and sends students to the wrong rule for the wrong reason.

subject: Teaching Reading
stem: A third-grade teacher wants students to understand how suffixes change the way a word works in a sentence. Which activity best targets that goal?
choices: Having students read multisyllabic words by dividing them into syllables
Having students look up base words in a dictionary and record the definitions
Having students practice reading words with the suffix -ed, focusing on its three pronunciations
Having students sort words ending in -ness, -ful, and -less according to the part of speech each suffix creates
correct_answer: Having students sort words ending in -ness, -ful, and -less according to the part of speech each suffix creates
explanation: The question requires an understanding of morphological instruction. Sorting by the part of speech a suffix produces makes the grammatical work that suffixes do visible: -ness forms a noun, while -ful and -less form adjectives. Students see that changing the ending relocates the word within a sentence.

distractor_explanations.Having students read multisyllabic words: Substituting syllabication, which serves pronunciation, for morphological analysis, which serves meaning Dividing into syllables is a decoding procedure aimed at pronunciation. It directs attention to vowel patterns rather than to the meaningful units inside the word, so it does not address how suffixes change function.
distractor_explanations.Having students look up base words in a: Treating dictionary definition work as instruction in word structure Recording definitions treats each word as an isolated item to be looked up. It never asks students to compare base and affix, which is where the insight about how suffixes operate comes from.
distractor_explanations.Having students practice reading words w: Equating work on a suffix's pronunciation with work on its grammatical function The three pronunciations of -ed are a real decoding concern, but the activity targets sound, not function. Practicing pronunciation leaves untouched the question of what the suffix does to the word's role in a sentence.

subject: Teaching Reading
stem: A first-grade student reads "the" as "thuh-ee" in every sentence. Which instructional response best addresses the difficulty?
choices: Having the student practice reading a list of other words that begin with the /th/ digraph
Teaching "the" as an irregular high-frequency word by drawing attention to the part that does not follow the expected pattern
Asking the student to use the sentence meaning and picture to figure out the word
Providing additional phonemic awareness practice in blending two phonemes
correct_answer: Teaching "the" as an irregular high-frequency word by drawing attention to the part that does not follow the expected pattern
explanation: The question requires an understanding of how irregular high-frequency words are taught. The student is applying letter-sound knowledge and getting stuck on the vowel, so the response is to name the irregular part explicitly and let the student hold the rest by pattern. This is the heart-word approach: most of the word is regular, and only the tricky part needs to be learned by attention.

distractor_explanations.Having the student practice reading a li: Attributing a high-frequency word error to general phonics weakness instead of to the specific correspondence that failed The student already produces /th/ correctly. Practicing more /th/ words drills a skill the student has, while the vowel spelling that caused the error goes unaddressed.
distractor_explanations.Asking the student to use the sentence m: Substituting context guessing for the instant recognition that high-frequency words require Guessing from context lets the student produce a word sometimes, but it does not build recognition of this spelling. The student will meet "the" constantly and needs to know it on sight, not infer it anew each time.
distractor_explanations.Providing additional phonemic awareness: Misjudging an orthographic difficulty as a phonemic awareness deficit The student is already blending sounds in print and is doing it too thoroughly. The difficulty is knowing which spelling convention applies, which is an orthographic problem, not a phonemic awareness deficit.

subject: Teaching Reading
stem: A third-grade student still labors over high-frequency words such as "because" and "friend" during oral reading. The teacher has already taught the phonics patterns those words contain. Which next step best applies the principle of repeated exposure?
choices: Lengthening the oral reading passages so the student gets more total practice time
Having the student look up the words in a dictionary and copy the definitions
Embedding the words in short sentences the student rereads across several sessions until recognition is immediate
Having the student sort the words by their vowel spelling patterns
correct_answer: Embedding the words in short sentences the student rereads across several sessions until recognition is immediate
explanation: The question requires an understanding of how repeated exposure builds sight word recognition. Short sentences give the target words many quick, successful encounters spread across sessions, which is what moves a word from effortful decoding to instant recognition. The brevity matters: it lets the student meet the same word several times in one sitting without fatigue.

distractor_explanations.Lengthening the oral reading passages so: Equating total reading volume with repeated exposure to specific target words Longer passages increase total reading time but scatter the target words thinly. The student meets each one once or twice per session, which is well below the number of encounters needed to make recognition automatic.
distractor_explanations.Having the student look up the words in: Treating dictionary work on word meaning as a way to build automatic word recognition The student can almost certainly use these words in speech and knows what they mean. The breakdown is in retrieving the printed form quickly, and dictionary work leaves that untouched.
distractor_explanations.Having the student sort the words by the: Treating an analytic sorting task as practice in rapid word retrieval Sorting develops awareness of patterns in English spelling, which is valuable for other purposes, but it is an analytic task performed at leisure. Automatic recognition requires rapid retrieval of the whole word, and sorting does not train that.

subject: Teaching Reading
stem: A second-grade teacher wants students to understand the convention that /j/ is spelled g before e, i, and y but j before a, o, and u. Which activity best develops that understanding?
choices: Having students read a decodable text containing many /j/ words and then answer comprehension questions
Having students write a story that uses as many /j/ words as they can think of
Having students chorally read a list of words that begin with /j/
Having students sort "gem," "giant," "gym," "jog," and "jump" by the letter that spells /j/ and notice which vowel follows it
correct_answer: Having students sort "gem," "giant," "gym," "jog," and "jump" by the letter that spells /j/ and notice which vowel follows it
explanation: The question requires an understanding of how spelling conventions are made explicit. A word sort places contrasting examples side by side and asks students to look for what governs the choice, so they construct the generalization from evidence rather than receiving it as a statement to memorize.

distractor_explanations.Having students read a decodable text co: Assuming students will infer a spelling convention from encounters in text without explicit comparison Reading words in text and then answering questions about meaning keeps attention on the message. Nothing in the task asks students to look at the spellings, so most will finish without noticing the pattern at all.
distractor_explanations.Having students write a story that uses: Using free writing as a way to teach a spelling convention Free composition puts the focus on ideas and, in any case, pushes students toward words they can already spell. The teacher loses control of which examples appear, so the targeted contrast may never come up.
distractor_explanations.Having students chorally read a list of: Treating choral reading practice as instruction in a spelling convention Choral reading builds fluency and confidence with pronunciation. It involves no comparison of spellings and no reflection on why a given letter was chosen.

subject: Teaching Reading
stem: During a one-to-one conference, a first-grade student reads "stop" correctly and then says, "This word has four letters, so it must have four sounds." Which teacher response best elicits and develops the student's thinking?
choices: Telling the student that English words do not always match one letter to one sound and moving on
Asking the student to say the sounds one at a time while counting on fingers, then comparing that count with the number of letters
Giving the student a list of words beginning with the /st/ blend to read
Praising the student for reading the word and then reading the next word together
correct_answer: Asking the student to say the sounds one at a time while counting on fingers, then comparing that count with the number of letters
explanation: The question requires an understanding of how a conference can develop a student's thinking. The student has stated a testable hypothesis, so the teacher gives the student a way to test it: produce the sounds, count them, and set that count against the letter count. The student discovers the mismatch independently, which both corrects the rule and shows the student how to check future attempts.

distractor_explanations.Telling the student that English words d: Replacing guided inquiry with direct correction, leaving the student's own hypothesis untested This response is accurate but it terminates the thinking instead of extending it. The student hears a correction to memorize rather than testing a personal hypothesis, so the underlying idea may survive alongside the new statement.
distractor_explanations.Giving the student a list of words begin: Substituting practice for conversation and leaving the student's stated reasoning unaddressed The student already read /st/ accurately, so blend practice addresses nothing the student got wrong. More importantly, it abandons the student's idea instead of engaging with it.
distractor_explanations.Praising the student for reading the wor: Using praise and reading along to avoid confronting a misconception Praise plus moving ahead leaves the mistaken rule intact and unexamined. The student will go on applying it to "ship," "that," and "chop" and misread every one of them.

subject: Teaching Reading
stem: A second-grade teacher is teaching students how to divide words into syllables while reading. Which sequence best supports students in applying syllabication independently?
choices: Teaching students to locate the vowel in each syllable, try the common division patterns, and then check whether the result sounds like a word they know
Having students clap out the beats in spoken words and then read the same words
Having students memorize the names of the six syllable types
Having students look up unfamiliar words in a dictionary to find the division points
correct_answer: Teaching students to locate the vowel in each syllable, try the common division patterns, and then check whether the result sounds like a word they know
explanation: The question requires an understanding of instructional strategies for syllabication. A usable strategy has to be a procedure, not just a fact: find the vowel, try a plausible division, and evaluate the attempt against oral vocabulary. The final check gives students a way to self-correct when the first division does not work.

distractor_explanations.Having students clap out the beats in sp: Treating clapped beats in spoken words as equivalent to dividing written words into syllables Clapping beats works on spoken syllables, and it does not transfer cleanly to print because spoken syllabication and written division often disagree on consonant placement. Students need a procedure anchored to letters, not to rhythm.
distractor_explanations.Having students memorize the names of th: Equating knowledge of syllable-type names with having a procedure for dividing words Naming the syllable types is vocabulary learning about reading, not the ability to divide a word. A student may label a syllable correctly and still have no procedure for deciding where one syllable ends and the next begins.
distractor_explanations.Having students look up unfamiliar words: Substituting a reference tool for the independent strategy students need to learn A dictionary supplies an answer for one word at a time and is unavailable during most reading. Depending on it leaves students with no independent way to attack an unfamiliar word.

subject: Teaching Reading
stem: A second-grade student reads "careless" and says, "It means full of care." Which next step best addresses the misunderstanding?
choices: Having the student reread the sentence and use the picture to confirm the meaning
Having the student divide "careless" into syllables and blend each part
Having the student compare "careless," "careful," and "hopeless" and discuss what -less and -ful add to a base word
Having the student write a sentence using the word "care"
correct_answer: Having the student compare "careless," "careful," and "hopeless" and discuss what -less and -ful add to a base word
explanation: The question requires an understanding of morphological instruction. The student has confused two suffixes with opposite meanings, so setting "careless" beside "careful" makes the contrast visible, and adding "hopeless" shows that the same suffix does the same work on a different base. The student constructs the meaning of -less rather than being told it.

distractor_explanations.Having the student reread the sentence a: Using context to confirm meaning instead of correcting the suffix meaning directly Context might steer the student to an acceptable guess this time, but it does not correct the suffix confusion. The student will attach the same wrong meaning to the next -less word that appears without a helpful picture.
distractor_explanations.Having the student divide \"careless\" i: Using syllabication to address an error in morphological meaning Syllable division addresses pronunciation, and the student already read the word accurately. The error is in meaning, so a decoding routine leaves it completely untouched.
distractor_explanations.Having the student write a sentence usin: Practicing the base word while leaving the suffix that caused the error unexamined Practicing the base word reinforces what the student already understands. The breakdown is entirely in the suffix, and this activity never asks the student to look at it.

subject: Teaching Reading
stem: In a small-group lesson, a third-grade student reads "farm-er" with a pause between the parts and then says "farmer." Which next step best extends the student's word-analysis skill?
choices: Asking the student to write "farmer" three times from memory
Asking the student to use "farmer" in a sentence to show understanding of its meaning
Asking the student to read a list of single-syllable words that begin with the same consonant blend
Asking the student to read other two-syllable words with the same closed-syllable pattern, such as "winter" and "sister"
correct_answer: Asking the student to read other two-syllable words with the same closed-syllable pattern, such as "winter" and "sister"
explanation: The question requires an understanding of how to move a partial success forward. The student has found the syllable boundary and applied a closed-syllable attempt to both parts. Giving several more words with the same structure consolidates the procedure at the same level of difficulty and builds the fluency that lets it become automatic.

distractor_explanations.Asking the student to write \"farmer\" t: Treating repeated copying and writing from memory as a way to build decoding skill Writing from memory exercises recall of one spelling. It does not give the student a repeatable procedure for words not yet practiced, so it adds nothing to word analysis.
distractor_explanations.Asking the student to use \"farmer\" in: Taking work on word meaning as the next step when the difficulty is orthographic analysis The student understood the word well enough to blend it into a real word. Meaning was never the obstacle, so a comprehension-focused follow-up leaves the developing skill unpracticed.
distractor_explanations.Asking the student to read a list of sin: Reducing task difficulty instead of consolidating a newly emerging strategy Single-syllable words with the same blend are easier than what the student just did. Moving backward forfeits the chance to consolidate the two-syllable strategy at the moment it is emerging.

subject: Teaching Reading
stem: A first-grade teacher wants her students to recognize irregular high-frequency words such as "said," "was," and "of" automatically. Which instructional approach best reflects how these words are learned?
choices: Requiring students to blend the letters sound by sound each time they meet the word
Providing brief, repeated exposures in which students read the word in a phrase, say the letters as they write it, and meet it again in connected text
Delaying these words until students have mastered every major phonics pattern
Having students copy each word ten times and then take a weekly spelling test
correct_answer: Providing brief, repeated exposures in which students read the word in a phrase, say the letters as they write it, and meet it again in connected text
explanation: The question requires an understanding of instructional techniques that expand recognition of words that are not fully decodable. Irregular words are learned through orthographic mapping: repeated, attention-focused encounters that connect the letters in sequence to the pronunciation. Brief practice that combines reading, saying, and writing, spread across days and reinforced in connected text, supplies the exposures that mapping requires.

distractor_explanations.Requiring students to blend the letters: Assuming irregular high-frequency words can be sounded out letter by letter, which rehearses a nonword pronunciation Blending is the right strategy for decodable words, but words such as "said" contain letters that do not follow the expected pattern. Asking students to sound them out each time teaches them to produce a nonword and never builds automatic recognition.
distractor_explanations.Delaying these words until students have: Assuming foundational skills must proceed in a strict linear order, with every phonics pattern mastered before high-frequency words appear These words carry a large share of beginning texts, so postponing them leaves students unable to read the very material used to practice phonics. Instruction in phonics patterns and in high-frequency words has to proceed together.
distractor_explanations.Having students copy each word ten times: Equating massed copying with repeated exposure, overlooking that copying draws attention away from the letter sequence and supplies no feedback Massed copying directs attention to filling rows rather than to the letter sequence that must be mapped to memory, and a weekly test checks recall without building automaticity. Effective exposure is brief, distributed, and focused on the word's spelling-sound connection.

subject: Teaching Reading
stem: A first-grade teacher puts the words "cat," "kite," "back," and "school" on the board and asks students what all four have in common. This activity primarily develops students' understanding that
choices: the same sound can be spelled with different letters or letter combinations
every syllable must contain a vowel
two consonants printed together are pronounced as one blended sound
a single letter can stand for more than one sound
correct_answer: the same sound can be spelled with different letters or letter combinations
explanation: The question requires an understanding of how letter-sound correspondences and spelling conventions are taught. All four words contain the sound /k/, but it is spelled c, k, ck, and ch. Noticing that one phoneme can be written several ways gives students flexibility when they meet an unfamiliar spelling, which is the point of comparing the words rather than drilling one pattern in isolation.

distractor_explanations.every syllable must contain a vowel: Reaching for an unrelated true fact about syllables instead of reading the pattern the word set was built to show The claim about syllables is true but unrelated to what these words share. Selecting it means answering from a familiar-sounding fact instead of from the pattern the teacher built the word set to show.
distractor_explanations.two consonants printed together are pron: Mistaking a digraph, which represents one sound, for a consonant cluster, in which both sounds are heard The final ck in "back" and the ch in "school" are digraphs representing a single sound, not clusters in which both consonants are heard. Treating them as blends would leave students expecting to produce two sounds.
