distractor_explanations.a single letter can stand for more than: Confusing the two directions of letter-sound correspondence: one phoneme with several spellings versus one letter with several sounds The letter-to-sound question, such as c saying /k/ or /s/, is a different concept from the sound-to-spelling question this set poses. All four words share one sound, so the target is the spelling side of the correspondence, not the variability of one letter's pronunciation.

subject: Teaching Reading
stem: At the start of second grade, Ms. Boyd asks each student to read aloud a list of pseudowords such as "vop," "sabe," and "flim." What does this measure most directly tell her?
choices: How well students understand the grade-level passages they read independently
How well students apply letter-sound knowledge to read words they have never seen
How many words students can recognize instantly, without sounding them out
How large each student's oral vocabulary is
correct_answer: How well students apply letter-sound knowledge to read words they have never seen
explanation: The question requires an understanding of what decoding measures assess. The words are pronounceable but meaningless, so students cannot draw on memory or context and must map graphemes to phonemes. The score therefore isolates the alphabetic principle and blending, which is exactly what a teacher needs before deciding how much phonics review the class requires.

distractor_explanations.How well students understand the grade-l: Treating a decoding measure as a measure of reading comprehension, which pseudoword reading cannot assess Passage comprehension depends on language comprehension as well as word recognition, and this measure removes meaning entirely. A student can decode pseudowords well and still comprehend poorly, or the reverse.
distractor_explanations.How many words students can recognize in: Equating quick word reading with instant sight recognition, even though pseudowords cannot be stored in memory Sight vocabulary is measured with real words that students have previously encountered. Pseudowords cannot be stored in memory, so reading them necessarily draws on decoding rather than on instant recognition.
distractor_explanations.How large each student's oral vocabulary: Conflating oral vocabulary size with word-level decoding ability Oral vocabulary is a language comprehension ability that grows through talk and experience, not through print-to-sound mapping. A student with a rich vocabulary may still score low here if alphabetic decoding is not yet secure.

subject: Teaching Reading
stem: Ms. Nakamura is planning a second-grade lesson on r-controlled vowels. Which sequence of steps best reflects explicit, systematic phonics instruction?
choices: Naming the pattern and modeling it with a think-aloud, guiding students to blend and sort words with the pattern, then having them read those words in decodable sentences
Having students read a trade book and underline every word containing "ar," "or," or "er" so that they can discover the pattern themselves
Teaching all of the r-controlled spellings in one lesson so that students see the complete set at once
Posting the week's r-controlled words on the word wall for students to memorize before they read them in text
correct_answer: Naming the pattern and modeling it with a think-aloud, guiding students to blend and sort words with the pattern, then having them read those words in decodable sentences
explanation: The question requires an understanding of how common phonics patterns are taught. Effective lessons release responsibility gradually: the teacher names the pattern and demonstrates it, students practice blending and sorting with guidance, and then they apply the pattern while reading connected text. Each step prepares the next, so students finish able to use the pattern rather than only recite it.

distractor_explanations.Having students read a trade book and un: Assuming that discovering a pattern in authentic text can substitute for explicit modeling and guided practice Unguided discovery asks students to infer a rule they have not been taught, and many will underline words that simply happen to contain those letters. Authentic text is a good place to apply a pattern, but a weak place to introduce one.
distractor_explanations.Teaching all of the r-controlled spellin: Assuming that teaching an entire family of spellings at once accelerates learning rather than overloading working memory Presenting ar, or, er, ir, and ur together overloads working memory and invites confusion among spellings that sound alike. Systematic instruction secures one pattern, then contrasts it with the next.
distractor_explanations.Posting the week's r-controlled words on: Substituting whole-word memorization for pattern instruction, which leaves students unable to decode untaught words Memorizing the posted words yields recognition of those words only. The purpose of teaching a vowel pattern is to hand students a tool for the untaught words they will meet later.

subject: Teaching Reading
stem: A third-grade student reads the word "robot" with a short o in the first syllable, pronouncing it "rob-ot." Which instructional move best addresses this error?
choices: Directing the student to look for a prefix such as re- or pre- at the beginning of the word
Encouraging the student to read the word more quickly so that it comes out right
Teaching the student to try the long vowel sound when a syllable ends with a single vowel
Having the student memorize the pronunciation of "robot"
correct_answer: Teaching the student to try the long vowel sound when a syllable ends with a single vowel
explanation: The question requires an understanding of how syllable types guide vowel pronunciation in longer words. The first syllable of "robot" is open, meaning it ends with a vowel, and open syllables usually take the long vowel sound. Teaching students to flex the vowel, trying the long sound when the short one yields no real word, gives them a strategy that transfers to every open syllable they meet.

distractor_explanations.Directing the student to look for a pref: Mistaking the vowel letter of an open syllable for a prefix, confusing syllable boundaries with morpheme boundaries The opening letters form the first syllable of the base word, not a meaning-bearing prefix. Instruction that blurs morpheme boundaries with syllable boundaries leads students to invent prefixes that do not exist.
distractor_explanations.Encouraging the student to read the word: Treating increased reading rate as a remedy for inaccurate vowel selection Rate is a remedy for slow reading, not for inaccurate reading. Reading faster simply produces the wrong vowel more quickly and trains the student to skip the analysis.
distractor_explanations.Having the student memorize the pronunci: Resorting to memorization for a fully decodable word and forgoing a transferable syllable-type strategy "Robot" follows a regular pattern, so memorizing it treats a teachable word as though it were irregular. The student would face the same problem again with "tiger" and "music."

subject: Teaching Reading
stem: A fourth-grade teacher writes "kindness," "careless," and "darkness" on the board and asks students what the three words have in common. This activity primarily develops students' ability to
choices: identify the final consonant sound in each base word
apply the closed-syllable pattern to multisyllabic words
use context clues to work out the meaning of unfamiliar words
use the suffix -ness to recognize that each word names a quality or state
correct_answer: use the suffix -ness to recognize that each word names a quality or state
explanation: The question requires an understanding of how morphemic analysis is taught. The suffix -ness turns an adjective into a noun naming a quality or condition, so recognizing it lets students read and interpret a whole family of words at once. Comparing words that share one suffix makes the pattern visible instead of leaving each word to be learned separately.

distractor_explanations.identify the final consonant sound in ea: Staying at the letter-sound level and overlooking the meaning-bearing morpheme the three words share The ending sounds of these three words are not the same, and the final consonant of each base word is not what the set was chosen to show. Attention at the sound level misses the meaningful unit the teacher selected the words for.
distractor_explanations.apply the closed-syllable pattern to mul: Treating a morphological task as syllabic decoding, which pronounces a word without explaining its meaning or part of speech Syllable patterns help a student pronounce a long word, but they say nothing about what the suffix contributes to meaning or to part of speech. Decoding gets the word off the page; morphology is what makes sense of it.
distractor_explanations.use context clues to work out the meanin: Substituting context-clue strategies for morphological analysis, a workaround that fails with unfamiliar derived words Context can sometimes hint at a meaning, but it is unreliable and does not travel: the -ness pattern serves students in any text. Morphological analysis is direct instruction in meaning, whereas context is a workaround.

subject: Teaching Reading
stem: Before his fifth-grade class reads a science article containing "photosynthesis," "chlorophyll," and "chloroplast," Mr. Osei wants to use those words to build vocabulary through direct instruction. Which move best integrates word analysis with that goal?
choices: Having students read the article independently and infer each term's meaning from context as they go
Teaching what photo-, chlor-, and -phyll mean, then guiding students to split the words into parts and check their meanings against the text
Giving students the definitions to copy before reading so that no instructional time is lost later
Asking each student to look up one word in the dictionary and write a sentence using it
correct_answer: Teaching what photo-, chlor-, and -phyll mean, then guiding students to split the words into parts and check their meanings against the text
explanation: The question requires an understanding of how word analysis carries direct vocabulary instruction. Teaching the recurring Greek elements and then having students take the words apart gives them a reusable key, since photo- and chlor- reappear in "photograph" and "chlorine." Checking the parts against the text ties the analysis to meaning instead of leaving it as a puzzle.

distractor_explanations.Having students read the article indepen: Assuming vocabulary is acquired incidentally through wide reading and context, without direct instruction Context in a dense science article rarely supplies enough information to fix a precise technical meaning, and students left to infer often settle on a vague or wrong sense. Incidental learning from context is slow and uneven; these words are worth teaching directly.
distractor_explanations.Giving students the definitions to copy: Equating handing students definitions with direct vocabulary instruction, skipping the active processing of word parts Handing over definitions is efficient but shallow: students receive words they have no way to unpack, so the knowledge does not extend to new words. Direct vocabulary instruction requires active processing of word parts and multiple meaningful encounters.
distractor_explanations.Asking each student to look up one word: Treating dictionary lookup as vocabulary teaching, since copying isolated definitions builds no analytical skill Dictionary definitions for technical terms are often harder than the words themselves, and copying one produces no analysis. The value of this word set lies in its shared parts, which a dictionary lookup leaves invisible.

subject: Teaching Reading
stem: A kindergarten teacher reviews a high-frequency word list and notices that many entries, such as "can," "did," and "not," follow predictable phonics patterns. Which decision best reflects that observation?
choices: Teach the decodable words through their letter-sound patterns and give extra attention to the irregular ones, such as "the" and "said"
Teach every word on the list as a whole shape to be memorized
Drop the decodable words from the list because students will pick them up through reading
Postpone all high-frequency word instruction until students know every consonant and short-vowel sound
correct_answer: Teach the decodable words through their letter-sound patterns and give extra attention to the irregular ones, such as "the" and "said"
explanation: The question requires an understanding of how high-frequency word instruction is differentiated. Words that follow the patterns being taught are best learned through those patterns, which reinforces the phonics lesson and shows students that decoding pays off. Words that break the patterns need the additional step of attention to the irregular letters, so sorting the list by decodability sends effort where it is actually needed.

distractor_explanations.Teach every word on the list as a whole: Assuming every high-frequency word must be memorized as a whole shape, wasting the chance to reinforce decodable patterns Treating every word as a shape to memorize ignores the letter-sound knowledge the student already has. Many frequent words are fully decodable and are better used as practice with the patterns being taught.
distractor_explanations.Drop the decodable words from the list b: Assuming frequent words will be absorbed through reading alone and therefore need no explicit instruction Removing words from instruction leaves their learning to chance, and the students who struggle most with print are the least likely to absorb them incidentally. Frequent exposure in text supports instruction; it does not replace it.
distractor_explanations.Postpone all high-frequency word instruc: Assuming foundational skills must follow a strict linear sequence instead of developing in parallel High-frequency words appear throughout the very texts used to practice letter-sound knowledge, so waiting means students cannot read the practice material. Decoding instruction and high-frequency word instruction reinforce each other from the beginning.

subject: Teaching Reading
stem: A second-grade student consistently writes "sed" for "said" and "wuz" for "was." Which instructional technique best addresses this pattern of errors?
choices: Accepting the spellings as a normal stage and waiting for the student to outgrow them
Providing additional phonics practice with short-vowel patterns
Pointing out the part of the word that does not sound the way it looks while the student says and writes it, then reviewing it briefly over several days
Having the student read longer decodable texts to build fluency
correct_answer: Pointing out the part of the word that does not sound the way it looks while the student says and writes it, then reviewing it briefly over several days
explanation: The question requires an understanding of how irregular high-frequency words are taught. The student is applying sound-out spelling to letters that do not follow the rule, so the fix is to make the irregular part explicit: name the part that does not match, have the student say and write the whole word while attending to that sequence, and return to it on several days so the spelling is mapped to memory.

distractor_explanations.Accepting the spellings as a normal stag: Extending developmental spelling theory to the point of never correcting the conventional spelling of common words Approximations are useful evidence in the earliest stage of writing, but by second grade these very common words should be conventional. Waiting leaves a high-frequency word wrong in everything the student writes.
distractor_explanations.Providing additional phonics practice wi: Reading misspelled irregular words as a phonics deficit when the student is in fact overapplying sound-out spelling The student already knows the short-vowel patterns well enough to produce these spellings, so more phonics practice would strengthen the very habit that is causing the error. The gap is knowledge of particular irregular words, not of sound-symbol patterns.
distractor_explanations.Having the student read longer decodable: Assuming additional decoding practice will incidentally correct the spelling of irregular high-frequency words Decodable texts contain regular words by design, so more time in them provides no practice with the words being misspelled. Fluency with patterns and memory for irregular words develop through different kinds of practice.

subject: Teaching Reading
stem: A first-grade student spells "back" as "bak" and "duck" as "duk." Which spelling convention should the teacher address?
choices: The letter k is used only before e, i, and y
Every final consonant sound is spelled with two letters
Doubled letters always signal that the vowel before them is short
The /k/ sound at the end of a one-syllable word with a short vowel is usually spelled ck rather than k
correct_answer: The /k/ sound at the end of a one-syllable word with a short vowel is usually spelled ck rather than k
explanation: The question requires an understanding of the spelling conventions that govern common letter-sound correspondences. The sound /k/ has several spellings, and English uses ck rather than k immediately after a short vowel in a one-syllable word. Teaching the convention directly gives the student a rule that covers dozens of words instead of a separate correction for each.

distractor_explanations.The letter k is used only before e, i, a: Merging two distinct conventions into one: the positional c-or-k rule and the final ck rule The statement about e, i, and y governs whether to write c or k, not whether k should be doubled. Applying it here would leave the student still writing "bak."
distractor_explanations.Every final consonant sound is spelled w: Overgeneralizing a narrow convention into a rule that every final consonant sound is spelled with two letters Most final consonant sounds are spelled with a single letter, as in "bat" and "run." An overgeneralized rule like this one would create new errors in words the student currently spells correctly.
distractor_explanations.Doubled letters always signal that the v: Extending the floss rule for doubling final f, l, and s to all consonants Doubling f, l, and s at the end of a short-vowel word is a separate convention from the ck rule. Treating doubled letters as a universal signal of a short vowel sends the student looking for double letters English does not use.

subject: Teaching Reading
stem: A first-grade teacher models blending "stop." Several students read it back as "suh-tuh-op." Which instructional point best addresses the error?
choices: Telling students to say the sounds in a continuous stream without adding a vowel after each consonant
Explaining that s and t form a digraph that stands for a single sound
Having students memorize "stop" as a sight word
Switching to words with final clusters because those are easier to blend
correct_answer: Telling students to say the sounds in a continuous stream without adding a vowel after each consonant
explanation: The question requires an understanding of how consonant clusters are taught. The students are inserting a schwa after each consonant, which happens when sounds are produced in isolation and then placed side by side. Directing them to hold and slide the sounds together, keeping the mouth ready for the next one, produces the cluster without added vowels and transfers to every word with an initial cluster.

distractor_explanations.Explaining that s and t form a digraph t: Mistaking a consonant cluster, in which both sounds are heard, for a digraph representing a single sound A digraph such as sh or ch represents one phoneme, but in "stop" both /s/ and /t/ are heard. Calling the pair a digraph would teach students to drop a sound the word actually contains.
distractor_explanations.Having students memorize \"stop\" as a s: Bypassing cluster blending by memorizing individual words, which teaches one word rather than a whole class of words Memorizing one word avoids the skill these students lack. They would then need to memorize "flag," "brick," and every other cluster word separately, and their blending would stay incomplete.
distractor_explanations.Switching to words with final clusters b: Changing which words are taught instead of correcting the faulty blending procedure Changing the word list does not address the inserted vowels, which will appear in final clusters too. The difficulty lies in the blending procedure, not in where the cluster sits in the word.

subject: Teaching Reading
stem: Ms. Whitfield wants an activity that develops students' thinking about syllable types rather than their ability to label them. Which activity best achieves that goal?
choices: Having students color-code open and closed syllables on a worksheet
Having students read pairs such as "fin" and "fine" and explain why the vowel sound changes
Having students copy the six syllable types onto a classroom chart
Having students sort words by the number of syllables they contain
correct_answer: Having students read pairs such as "fin" and "fine" and explain why the vowel sound changes
explanation: The question requires an understanding of how activities are evaluated by the thinking they demand. Comparing "fin" and "fine" and explaining the change obliges students to reason about the mechanism: the silent e reaches back and makes the vowel long. The activity turns the rule into something students can state and test, which is exactly the reasoning that labeling practice does not require.

distractor_explanations.Having students color-code open and clos: Equating identification and labeling with understanding a mechanism, since color-coding requires no explanation Color-coding asks students to classify, and a student can classify correctly by matching a familiar pattern without being able to say why the vowel is long. The activity checks recognition of a category, not reasoning about how the category works.
distractor_explanations.Having students copy the six syllable ty: Equating the production of a classroom display with learning, as transcription demands no cognitive processing Copying definitions onto a chart is transcription. It produces a reference display but requires no engagement with how syllable types affect pronunciation.
distractor_explanations.Having students sort words by the number: Confusing counting syllables with classifying syllable types, a matter of number rather than of kind Counting syllables is a separate skill that says nothing about whether a syllable is open, closed, or vowel-consonant-e. Students could sort every word correctly and still be unable to use syllable type to decide a vowel sound.

subject: Teaching Reading
stem: When a third-grade student meets the unfamiliar word "basket," he says "baseball" and keeps reading. Which strategy instruction best addresses this behavior?
choices: Telling the student to use the illustrations to work out what the word must be
Having the student sound out only the first letter and then try a word that fits the sentence
Teaching the student to look all the way through the word, check the beginning, middle, and ending, and reread to see whether his reading makes sense
Encouraging the student to skip unfamiliar words and read on for the main idea
correct_answer: Teaching the student to look all the way through the word, check the beginning, middle, and ending, and reread to see whether his reading makes sense
explanation: The question requires an understanding of how word-solving strategies are taught in the intermediate grades. The student is substituting a word that shares only the first letters, so instruction should make the whole letter sequence the object of attention and add a check: does what I said look right and make sense? Rereading turns the error into something the student can catch himself.

distractor_explanations.Telling the student to use the illustrat: Relying on illustrations and other non-print cues to guess words instead of analyzing letter-sound correspondences Pictures can suggest a topic but rarely identify a specific word, and they do nothing in the many texts without illustrations. Reliance on them leaves students with no way to solve words in text alone.
distractor_explanations.Having the student sound out only the fi: Accepting partial decoding that sounds out only the first letter and then guesses, leaving the student no way to self-check Starting with one letter and guessing produces substitutions exactly like this student's, because many words begin the same way. Partial decoding weakens accurate word solving rather than supporting it.
distractor_explanations.Encouraging the student to skip unfamili: Accepting the skipping of unknown words as a legitimate strategy, which abandons word meaning and lets errors accumulate Skipping leaves the sentence incomplete and trains the student to read past the very words that carry new information. Comprehension depends on the meanings that were skipped.

subject: Teaching Reading
stem: Ms. Alvarez notices that one of her kindergarten students blends unseen words accurately but rarely remembers words such as "was" and "they." Which technique best supports this student?
choices: Providing additional phonemic awareness practice in blending and segmenting
Having the student reread the same decodable book until the reading is fluent
Having the student copy the words during independent work time
Naming the part of the word that does not sound the way it looks while the student traces and says the word, followed by several short reviews in the same week
correct_answer: Naming the part of the word that does not sound the way it looks while the student traces and says the word, followed by several short reviews in the same week
explanation: The question requires an understanding of how multisensory techniques and repeated exposure build recognition of irregular words. The student can already decode, so the missing piece is orthographic mapping of words that break the rules. Naming the unexpected part, tracing and saying the word so several senses carry the same information, and returning to it briefly several times in one week creates the conditions for the spelling to stick.

distractor_explanations.Providing additional phonemic awareness: Attributing failure to retain high-frequency words to weak phonemic awareness when the real gap is orthographic mapping The student's blending is already accurate, so more phonemic awareness practice targets a strength rather than the difficulty. Remembering irregular words depends on mapping letters to memory, which is a different demand from hearing and manipulating sounds.
distractor_explanations.Having the student reread the same decod: Assuming repeated reading of decodable texts will incidentally teach the irregular high-frequency words those texts exclude by design Decodable books exclude exactly the irregular words this student needs, so rereading them offers no practice with "was" or "they." Repeated reading builds fluency with patterns; it does not teach irregular spellings.
distractor_explanations.Having the student copy the words during: Treating unsupervised copying as practice, with no attention to letter sequence and no feedback to stop errors from being rehearsed Copying without attention to the letter sequence produces handwriting practice, not learning, and errors are rehearsed rather than corrected. Effective practice is brief, guided, and aimed at the part of the word that must be remembered.

subject: Teaching Reading
stem: Ms. Ferraro notices that one of her second-grade students writes "plai" for "play" and "trai" for "tray" during writing workshop. Which generalization would best settle the choice for him?
choices: The long a spelled ay is used at the end of a word or syllable, while ai is used elsewhere
Every long vowel sound is spelled with two vowels working together
The letters a and i together always stand for the long a sound
Vowel teams must be memorized one at a time because English spelling follows no patterns
correct_answer: The long a spelled ay is used at the end of a word or syllable, while ai is used elsewhere
explanation: The question requires an understanding of the spelling conventions that govern common letter-sound correspondences. Both ai and ay represent long a, but English positionally prefers ay at the end of a word or syllable and ai elsewhere. Teaching the position rule lets the student choose between two spellings of the same sound instead of guessing.

distractor_explanations.Every long vowel sound is spelled with t: Overgeneralizing vowel teams as the only way to spell long vowels, ignoring silent e and open syllables Long vowels are also spelled with a silent e, as in "cake," or with a single vowel in an open syllable, as in "me." The overgeneralization leaves students puzzled by a large group of very common words.
distractor_explanations.The letters a and i together always stan: Treating one vowel team as the fixed spelling of a sound, ignoring competing spellings and positional constraints Treating ai as the automatic choice is the error the student is already making. The point of instruction is to show that several spellings compete for the same sound and that position decides among them.
distractor_explanations.Vowel teams must be memorized one at a t: Assuming English spelling is patternless and must be memorized word by word English spelling is regular enough to teach: most correspondences follow patterns, and teaching those patterns is far more efficient than memorizing words one at a time. Surrendering to memorization removes the most useful tool students can have.

subject: Teaching Reading
stem: Two English learners in a second-grade class score below benchmark on a pseudoword decoding measure but perform at grade level on a listening comprehension task. Which conclusion is best supported by these results?
choices: The students have a language-based comprehension problem that calls for intensive vocabulary instruction
The students' difficulty is at the level of word recognition, so decoding instruction is warranted and listening comprehension is a strength to build on
The screening is not valid for English learners and the results should be set aside
The students should be referred for special education evaluation before any instruction is changed
correct_answer: The students' difficulty is at the level of word recognition, so decoding instruction is warranted and listening comprehension is a strength to build on
explanation: The question requires an understanding of how assessment data are interpreted for diverse learners. Pseudoword decoding draws little on English oral vocabulary, so a low score points to word recognition, while grade-level listening comprehension shows that language comprehension is developing normally. Together the two results locate the difficulty precisely and indicate that decoding instruction, not vocabulary intervention, is the next step.

distractor_explanations.The students have a language-based compr: Reading the assessment results backwards, since grade-level listening comprehension rules out a language-comprehension problem The listening comprehension data contradict this reading: the students understand language at grade level. Intensive vocabulary instruction would target the one area in which they are performing well.
distractor_explanations.The screening is not valid for English l: Assuming standardized screeners are invalid for English learners and discarding data that are in fact interpretable Because pseudowords carry no meaning, the measure does not penalize a smaller English vocabulary the way a passage reading task can. Setting aside valid information would leave a real decoding difficulty unaddressed.
distractor_explanations.The students should be referred for spec: Assuming a low screening score requires a special education referral before instruction is adjusted and the response monitored Screening data are meant to inform instruction first. A structured response of targeted decoding instruction with progress monitoring is the appropriate next step, and referral enters the picture only if students fail to respond.

subject: Teaching Reading
stem: A kindergarten teacher wants to build students' awareness of sound patterns at the word level before moving on to work with individual phonemes. Which oral activity best targets this goal?
choices: Asking students to replace the first sound in "map" with /t/ and say the new word
Asking students to identify the first sound they hear in the word "sun"
Asking students to decide whether two spoken words, such as "cat" and "hat," end with the same sound
Asking students to blend the sounds /c/ /a/ /t/ to say a single word
correct_answer: Asking students to decide whether two spoken words, such as "cat" and "hat," end with the same sound
explanation: The question requires an understanding of systematic and explicit methods for teaching phonological awareness. Rhyme recognition asks students to compare the ending sounds of whole words, which develops awareness of sound patterns at the word level (onset-rime) rather than at the level of individual phonemes. Because it does not require isolating or manipulating single sounds, it is an appropriate foundation to establish before phonemic awareness work begins.

distractor_explanations.Asking students to replace the first sou: Confusing phoneme substitution, the most demanding kind of sound manipulation, with an entry-level awareness task, which flattens the hierarchy of skills. Phoneme substitution is one of the most advanced phonemic awareness tasks, requiring students to hold a word in memory, delete a sound, and insert another. It is far beyond a starting point for students who have not yet developed word-level awareness.
distractor_explanations.Asking students to identify the first so: Equating first-sound identification at the phoneme level with word-level work. Hearing one sound is not the same as comparing the sound patterns of whole words. Identifying the first sound in a word is phoneme isolation, which operates at the individual sound level rather than the word level. It belongs to the later phase of instruction the teacher is preparing for, not the foundational phase described.
distractor_explanations.Asking students to blend the sounds /c/: Confusing phoneme blending with word-level phonological awareness, and so skipping the developmental sequence from whole words down to individual sounds. Blending individual phonemes to form a word is phonemic awareness, the level the teacher plans to move to later. It requires students to hold and combine separate sounds, which is more demanding than comparing whole-word endings and skips the foundational step the teacher is targeting.

subject: Teaching Reading
stem: A teacher gives each student three counters and says, "Push one counter forward for every sound you hear in 'cat.'" Which skill is this activity designed to develop?
choices: Phonics, because students are attending to the sounds that letters represent
Reading fluency, because students are practicing accurate and rapid word recognition
Reading comprehension, because students must know what the word means to complete the task
Phonemic awareness, because students are segmenting a spoken word into its individual phonemes
correct_answer: Phonemic awareness, because students are segmenting a spoken word into its individual phonemes
explanation: The question requires an understanding of how phonemic awareness is taught. Moving a counter for each sound heard is phoneme segmentation, a core phonemic awareness skill: students manipulate individual sounds in spoken words without any print involved.

distractor_explanations.Phonics, because students are attending: Treating any activity that involves speech sounds as phonics. Phonics is about print-to-sound mapping; phonemic awareness is purely auditory and can be done with the eyes closed. Phonics instruction teaches the correspondence between letters (graphemes) and sounds (phonemes), so it requires printed text. In this activity no letters appear at all, and students work entirely by listening.
distractor_explanations.Reading fluency, because students are pr: Using fluency as a catch-all label for any difficulty observed during reading. Fluency operates at the level of connected text, not single spoken words. Fluency means reading connected text accurately, at an appropriate rate, and with prosody. This task uses no text and asks nothing about rate or expression, so it cannot build fluency.
distractor_explanations.Reading comprehension, because students: Classifying every reading-related task as comprehension. Phonemic awareness sits below word recognition and is a prerequisite for it, not a product of it. Comprehension is the construction of meaning from text. Segmenting the sounds in 'cat' happens at the sound level; a student can complete it successfully without knowing what a cat is.

subject: Teaching Reading
stem: A kindergarten teacher says, "Listen: /k/ /a/ /t/ is 'cat.' Now let's change the first sound to /b/. What word do we have?" Which phonemic awareness skill is the teacher targeting?
choices: Phoneme isolation
Phoneme substitution
Phoneme deletion
Syllable blending
correct_answer: Phoneme substitution
explanation: The question requires an understanding of the phonemic awareness skill progression. Replacing the initial phoneme of a word to produce a new word is phoneme substitution, a more advanced manipulation skill typically taught after blending and segmenting are secure.

distractor_explanations.Phoneme isolation: Equating any task that names a first sound with isolation. Isolation identifies; substitution manipulates. Phoneme isolation asks students to identify the sound in a given position, as in "What is the first sound in 'cat'?" Here the teacher supplies the sound and asks students to swap it, which is one level harder.
distractor_explanations.Phoneme deletion: Confusing removing a phoneme with replacing one. Both change the word, but only deletion leaves the position empty. Deletion would ask "Say 'cat.' Now say it without /k/." That removes a sound entirely and leaves 'at.' This task replaces /k/ with /b/ to make 'bat,' so a sound remains in that position.
distractor_explanations.Syllable blending: Confusing the syllable level with the phoneme level of the sound structure hierarchy. Syllable blending combines larger units of sound, as in blending 'pic' and 'nic' into 'picnic.' The word 'cat' is a single syllable, and the teacher is working at the phoneme level, below the syllable.

subject: Teaching Reading
stem: During an informal assessment, a teacher asks a first grader to blend the sounds /d/ /o/ /g/. The student responds "d... o... g... doh." Which statement best describes the student's difficulty?
choices: The student cannot blend individual phonemes into a word, an undeveloped phonemic awareness skill
The student has acquired the alphabetic principle but lacks sight word recognition
The student has a speech sound production disorder that interferes with decoding
The student reads with insufficient fluency to support comprehension
correct_answer: The student cannot blend individual phonemes into a word, an undeveloped phonemic awareness skill
explanation: The question requires an understanding of how to interpret informal assessment data. The student produces the phonemes in sequence but cannot fuse them into a word, which indicates a gap in blending, a foundational phonemic awareness skill that must precede successful decoding.

distractor_explanations.The student has acquired the alphabetic: Assuming that because a student can produce letter sounds, the alphabetic principle is in place. Producing sounds and blending them into a word are distinct achievements. Blending is precisely what the alphabetic principle requires. If the student could map letters to sounds and then fuse those sounds, the word would be read. Sight word recognition is a separate issue and is not what this response shows.
distractor_explanations.The student has a speech sound productio: Attributing a cognitive-linguistic gap to a speech or motor difficulty. Clear articulation in the response is the evidence that rules this out. The student articulated /d/, /o/, and /g/ clearly, which rules out a production problem. The breakdown is not in saying the sounds but in mentally combining them.
distractor_explanations.The student reads with insufficient flue: Applying a broad label such as fluency to any observed reading difficulty, which obscures the specific skill that needs teaching. Fluency concerns reading connected text with accuracy, rate, and prosody. This student has not yet blended a single spoken word, so the difficulty lies at a more basic level than fluency.

subject: Teaching Reading
stem: During a shared reading of a big book, Ms. Alvarez runs her finger beneath the words as she reads and pauses to say, "We finished this line, so we go back to the start of the next one." Which concept of print is she teaching?
choices: One-to-one match, the correspondence between each spoken word and a written word
Book orientation, the difference between the front cover and the back cover
Return sweep, the movement from the end of one line of print to the beginning of the next
Letter-sound correspondence, the match between a letter and the sound it represents
correct_answer: Return sweep, the movement from the end of one line of print to the beginning of the next
explanation: The question requires an understanding of how concepts of print are taught systematically and explicitly. Naming and modeling the return sweep draws attention to directionality: English print is read left to right and top to bottom, and reading resumes at the beginning of the next line. Beginning readers often invent their own route back to the left margin or skip the move entirely, so the behavior has to be shown rather than assumed.

distractor_explanations.One-to-one match, the correspondence bet: Reaches for one-to-one match, another genuine concept of print, without tying the choice to the teacher behavior the stem actually names. One-to-one match is also a concept of print, but it concerns pointing to each word as it is spoken. The teacher's comment is specifically about where reading resumes at the end of a line, which is a different concept.
distractor_explanations.Book orientation, the difference between: Defaults to book-orientation knowledge and skips the specific move described in the stem, resuming at the start of the next line. Book orientation is taught by identifying the front cover, the title page, and where reading begins. None of those elements appears in the scenario, and none is what the teacher is pointing to.
distractor_explanations.Letter-sound correspondence, the match b: Files letter-sound correspondence under concepts of print, a category that covers how text is arranged and works rather than which sounds letters stand for. Letter-sound correspondence belongs to the alphabetic principle, not to concepts of print, and it is not what the teacher's finger movement demonstrates. Nothing in the scenario connects a printed symbol to a sound.

subject: Teaching Reading
stem: Ms. Byrne holds up a card with the letter m and says, "This letter stands for the sound /m/. Listen for it at the beginning of mop and mom — the same letter stands for the same sound in both." This lesson introduces
choices: Phonemic awareness, the understanding that spoken words can be broken into individual sounds
Concepts of print, the understanding that text carries meaning and is read left to right
Sight recognition, the understanding that some words must be learned as whole units
The alphabetic principle, the understanding that written letters systematically represent the sounds in spoken words
correct_answer: The alphabetic principle, the understanding that written letters systematically represent the sounds in spoken words
explanation: The question requires an understanding of the alphabetic principle in early literacy instruction. The teacher is not merely asking students to hear /m/; she is linking a sound they hear to a printed symbol and showing that the same symbol recurs across different words. That mapping insight is what later lets students decode unfamiliar words instead of memorizing them one at a time.

distractor_explanations.Phonemic awareness, the understanding th: Stops at hearing the sound and misses the point that the alphabetic principle begins only when a printed symbol is mapped onto that sound. If the lesson stopped at hearing /m/ in two words, it would be phonemic awareness, an entirely oral skill. The letter card and the statement that the letter stands for the sound move the lesson into the alphabetic principle.
distractor_explanations.Concepts of print, the understanding tha: Reads the presence of a printed letter as concepts of print instruction, a category that says nothing about what a letter represents. Concepts of print concern how written language is organized and handled, such as directionality, spacing, and the parts of a book. They say nothing about what a letter represents.
distractor_explanations.Sight recognition, the understanding tha: Treats quick whole-word recognition as where early reading starts, when it is really what secure alphabetic mapping eventually produces and leaves students with no strategy for unfamiliar words. Sight recognition is a by-product of secure alphabetic mapping, not its starting point. Teaching children to memorize whole words first leaves them without a strategy for words they have never seen.

subject: Teaching Reading
stem: A kindergarten teacher replaces an alphabetized word wall with a sound wall that groups spellings by phoneme and includes mouth pictures. Which statement best describes the primary instructional purpose of this change?
choices: To give students a reference for connecting the sounds they hear to the spellings that represent those sounds
To give students a reference for spelling high-frequency words correctly during independent writing
To surround students with print so that repeated exposure produces letter and word learning
To help students learn the alphabet in order by consulting the display each day
correct_answer: To give students a reference for connecting the sounds they hear to the spellings that represent those sounds
explanation: The question requires an understanding of how classroom materials support specific instructional goals. A sound wall is organized by phoneme rather than by initial letter, so a student who hears a sound can locate it and find the graphemes that spell it. That organization supports both segmenting words for spelling and blending sounds while reading.

distractor_explanations.To give students a reference for spellin: Conflates a sound wall with a word wall: one is organized by phoneme to support sound-spelling mapping, the other alphabetically to support looking up whole words. That is the purpose of an alphabetized word wall of high-frequency or irregular words. Students consult such a wall for whole words, not for the relationship between a sound and its spellings, which is the work a sound wall supports.
distractor_explanations.To surround students with print so that: Assumes print on the walls does the teaching on its own, forgetting that a display helps only once students are shown how to use it. A print-rich room is worth having, but exposure alone does not teach sound-spelling relationships. A display supports learning only when students are taught how to use it and are referred to it during instruction.
distractor_explanations.To help students learn the alphabet in o: Equates knowing the alphabet in order with readiness to read, though reciting letters and knowing their sounds are separate bodies of knowledge. Reciting the alphabet in order is a different skill from knowing the sounds letters represent. A sound wall is deliberately organized by phoneme, not alphabetically, precisely so that it does not reinforce alphabetical order.

subject: Teaching Reading
stem: Ms. Lin says to her kindergarten class, "Say cupcake. Now say cupcake without saying cake." This task primarily develops students'
choices: Vocabulary, by having students analyze the meaningful parts of a compound word
Phonological awareness at the syllable level, by having students delete a syllable from a spoken word
Phonemic awareness, by having students delete an individual sound from a spoken word
Decoding, by having students take apart a printed word they have seen before
correct_answer: Phonological awareness at the syllable level, by having students delete a syllable from a spoken word
explanation: The question requires an understanding of how phonological awareness develops from larger to smaller units of sound. The unit being removed is a syllable, a large and easily heard chunk of speech, and the entire task is done by ear with no print involved. Oral deletion at this level is a strong predictor of later reading achievement and is typically taught before phoneme-level work.

distractor_explanations.Vocabulary, by having students analyze t: Follows the meaning of the compound instead of its sound structure; the task asks students to say something, not to explain it. The word is a compound and its parts do carry meaning, but the task directs attention to the sound structure of the word, not to what its parts mean. Students are asked to say something, not to explain it.
distractor_explanations.Phonemic awareness, by having students d: Takes any successful word-splitting as phoneme-level work, though a syllable is a much larger unit and far easier to detach than a single sound. The unit removed here is a syllable, not a single phoneme. A student who can drop cake from cupcake may still be unable to say cat without the /k/, which is the harder phoneme-level operation.
distractor_explanations.Decoding, by having students take apart: Hears taking a word apart as decoding, forgetting that decoding operates on printed words while this task never leaves the ear. Decoding works on printed text. This task is entirely oral, so it can neither build nor measure decoding ability, regardless of whether students have seen the word in a book.

subject: Teaching Reading
stem: Which read-aloud practice best promotes first-grade students' oral language development?
choices: Playing an audio recording of the story while students follow along in their own copies
Having students copy definitions of story words into a vocabulary notebook after the reading
Pausing to discuss a few target words, asking open-ended questions, and having students turn and talk with a partner
Reading the story aloud expressively from beginning to end while students listen quietly
correct_answer: Pausing to discuss a few target words, asking open-ended questions, and having students turn and talk with a partner
explanation: The question requires an understanding of how oral language is developed through instruction. An interactive read-aloud gives students a reason to produce language, supplies the words and sentence patterns they need, and then returns their attention to the text. Listening alone is receptive; the questions and the partner turn push students into expressive use of new vocabulary and syntax.

distractor_explanations.Playing an audio recording of the story: Mistakes following along with a recording for interaction, though no one responds to the student and nothing requires an answer. Following along in a text while a recording plays adds print tracking, but the experience stays passive. There is no interaction, no feedback, and no demand for the student to produce language.
distractor_explanations.Having students copy definitions of stor: Substitutes copying definitions for oral vocabulary growth, when words take hold only through repeated use in meaningful listening and speaking. Copying definitions is a writing task that treats words as list items. It gives no practice hearing the words in connected speech or using them in a sentence of the student's own.
distractor_explanations.Reading the story aloud expressively fro: Treats hearing plenty of language as the same thing as developing it, overlooking that receptive input must be paired with chances to produce language. Expressive reading models prosody and can support comprehension, but listening is receptive only. Students who never speak are not practicing the language they are hearing, so oral production does not grow.

subject: Teaching Reading
stem: A first-grade teacher is planning instruction in phoneme deletion. Which sequence reflects how the skill is best developed?
choices: Deleting the medial vowel first, because the vowel carries the most information about the identity of the word
Substituting one phoneme for another first, because substitution combines deletion and addition and is therefore more efficient
Presenting the words in writing so that students can see which letters to remove before they say the new word
Deleting the initial phoneme of a one-syllable word first, then the final phoneme, then one phoneme within a consonant cluster
correct_answer: Deleting the initial phoneme of a one-syllable word first, then the final phoneme, then one phoneme within a consonant cluster
explanation: The question requires an understanding of evidence-based sequences for phonemic awareness instruction. Deletion gets harder as the phoneme's position becomes harder to hold in memory: the first sound of a word is easiest to isolate, the final sound comes next, and removing one sound from a cluster such as the /s/ in stop means reconfiguring the whole onset. Teaching in that order keeps the task within reach while raising the demand.

distractor_explanations.Deleting the medial vowel first, because: Orders instruction by how much information a phoneme carries rather than by how hard it is to manipulate; medial vowels yield last, not first. Medial vowels are among the last phonemes children can manipulate, not the first, because the vowel sits between two consonants that must be held in memory while it is removed.
distractor_explanations.Substituting one phoneme for another fir: Takes the more complex operation as the more efficient one and skips the simpler deletion work that substitution is built on. Substitution is a later, harder operation because it requires holding the target word in memory while deleting and adding at the same time. Introducing it first skips the prerequisite step and the practice that builds it.
distractor_explanations.Presenting the words in writing so that: Believes phoneme work needs visible letters to lean on, though adding print turns an oral task into spelling or decoding. Removing printed letters turns the task into a spelling or decoding activity. Phonemic awareness work is oral by definition; adding print changes both what is being taught and what the response reveals.

subject: Teaching Reading
stem: Screening shows that most of Ms. Adeyemi's kindergarten class can produce rhymes and blend onsets and rimes, but only three students can segment the three phonemes in a word such as ship. Which response best reflects systematic and explicit instruction?
choices: Keeping the class moving through onset-rime work while adding a daily small-group routine that models phoneme segmentation, guides practice with counters, and reviews sounds already taught
Returning the whole class to rhyming and syllable work until every student has reached mastery of those levels
Waiting to address phonemes until students begin reading, since phonemic awareness develops as a result of reading print
Providing phoneme instruction only in one-on-one tutoring sessions and leaving it out of whole-class time
correct_answer: Keeping the class moving through onset-rime work while adding a daily small-group routine that models phoneme segmentation, guides practice with counters, and reviews sounds already taught
explanation: The question requires an understanding of how systematic and explicit instruction responds to assessment data. Systematic instruction follows a planned sequence, so the class continues at the onset-rime level while a small group gets the additional, more demanding work those three students need. Explicit instruction supplies the modeling, guided practice, and cumulative review that make the harder level learnable rather than assumed.

distractor_explanations.Returning the whole class to rhyming and: Reads holding the whole class until everyone masters a level as the careful choice, when systematic teaching advances on sequence and answers individual gaps in small groups. Holding the entire class at a level most students have already mastered postpones instruction the class is ready for, and it still does not give the three students what they are missing at the phoneme level.
distractor_explanations.Waiting to address phonemes until studen: Inverts the causal direction, assuming that reading print will hand students phonemic awareness rather than drawing on it as the foundation decoding requires. The causal direction runs the other way. Phonemic awareness supports learning to read, so waiting for reading to produce it inverts the relationship and leaves students without the foundation decoding requires.
distractor_explanations.Providing phoneme instruction only in on: Treats tiered support as a stand-in for core instruction instead of an addition layered on top of strong whole-class teaching. Tiered support adds to core instruction; it does not replace it. Removing phoneme work from the whole-class block leaves the class dependent on pull-out time that is usually too short to close the gap.

subject: Teaching Reading
stem: A kindergarten student names most uppercase letters correctly but rarely identifies their lowercase forms. Which instructional approach is most effective?
choices: Setting letter work aside and continuing oral language activities until the student shows more interest in letters
Teaching both forms together, pointing out that they share a name and a sound, and having the student match and sort uppercase and lowercase pairs
Teaching uppercase letters to mastery first and then introducing the lowercase forms one at a time
Having the student print both forms of each letter daily until letter formation becomes automatic
correct_answer: Teaching both forms together, pointing out that they share a name and a sound, and having the student match and sort uppercase and lowercase pairs
explanation: The question requires an understanding of how print concepts and letter knowledge are taught explicitly. Presenting the two cases together is efficient because the name and the sound stay constant while only the shape changes, which reduces the memory load. Matching and sorting pairs also prepares the student for the fact that running text is mostly lowercase, with capitals reserved for special uses.

distractor_explanations.Setting letter work aside and continuing: Treats readiness as something to wait for rather than something teaching builds, turning a documented need into a reason to postpone. Letter knowledge is taught, not waited for. Setting it aside removes an instructional opportunity instead of responding to what the assessment showed the student needs.
distractor_explanations.Teaching uppercase letters to mastery fi: Trusts a one-case-at-a-time sequence as the safe route, though withholding lowercase delays the form students meet most often in books. Delaying lowercase forms postpones work with the case students encounter most in books, and it can produce the very confusion the sequence is meant to prevent. Both cases can be learned at once.
distractor_explanations.Having the student print both forms of e: Equates the motor act of forming a letter with knowing it, as if a student who can print a letter can necessarily name it and give its sound. Handwriting practice builds letter formation and may reinforce recognition indirectly, but motor practice alone does not guarantee that a student can name the letter or recall its sound.

subject: Teaching Reading
stem: Ms. Pratt's kindergartners can blend the spoken sounds /k/ /a/ /t/ to say cat, but most of them cannot read the printed word cat. Which statement best explains this pattern?
choices: They need more oral blending practice before any printed letters are introduced
They need to memorize cat as a whole word before additional words are introduced
They have phonemic awareness but have not yet connected sounds to letters, so instruction should make that mapping explicit
Their phonemic awareness is not yet secure, as the inability to read the printed word shows
correct_answer: They have phonemic awareness but have not yet connected sounds to letters, so instruction should make that mapping explicit
explanation: The question requires an understanding of the alphabetic principle and how it is taught. Blending spoken sounds shows that students can work with phonemes by ear. Reading the printed word additionally requires knowing that those phonemes are represented by c, a, and t, and holding those mappings while blending. Explicit phonics work with letter tiles or sound boxes supplies the missing link.

distractor_explanations.They need more oral blending practice be: Holds that phonemic awareness must be complete before letters appear, when pairing sounds with letters during blending is what builds the alphabetic insight. Once students can blend orally, waiting to add letters delays decoding. Pairing sounds with letters during blending is exactly what builds the alphabetic insight, and it is more effective than more oral-only practice.
distractor_explanations.They need to memorize cat as a whole wor: Offers memorizing whole words in place of explicit mapping, mistaking a small stock of recognized words for the ability to read. Memorizing individual words gives students no strategy for words they have not been taught, which is precisely the problem the alphabetic principle solves.
distractor_explanations.Their phonemic awareness is not yet secu: Reads the failure with print backward as weak phonemic awareness, though oral blending is intact and the gap lies in sound-to-letter mapping. The evidence points the other way: these students blend spoken sounds successfully. Their difficulty appears only when print is involved, so the gap is in mapping, not in phonemic awareness.

subject: Teaching Reading
stem: Which sequence reflects the developmental progression of phonological awareness instruction in kindergarten and first grade?
choices: Individual phonemes first, because they are the smallest units and therefore the simplest to notice
Onset-rime work alone until students enter second grade, then individual phonemes
Syllables and individual phonemes taught together from the first week, since both involve breaking words apart
Awareness of words in sentences, then syllables, then onset and rime, then individual phonemes
correct_answer: Awareness of words in sentences, then syllables, then onset and rime, then individual phonemes
explanation: The question requires an understanding of how phonological awareness develops from larger to smaller units of sound. Children notice words in sentences and then syllables before they can attend to the rime of a word, and they handle onsets and rimes well before they can hold three separate phonemes in mind. Instruction that follows this progression lets each level rest on the one before it.

distractor_explanations.Individual phonemes first, because they: Takes smallest to mean simplest, inverting the real relation: the smaller the unit, the heavier the memory load and the harder the task. Smaller is harder, not simpler. Isolating the middle phoneme of a word requires holding the rest of the word in memory while removing one piece, a demand beginning students cannot yet meet.
distractor_explanations.Onset-rime work alone until students ent: Settles on onset-rime work as the destination rather than the bridge it is, leaving students short of the phonemic awareness decoding depends on. Onset-rime work is an important bridge, but stopping there for a year leaves students without the phonemic awareness that predicts decoding success and delays the phonics it is meant to support.
distractor_explanations.Syllables and individual phonemes taught: Groups every kind of word-taking-apart together, ignoring that syllables and phonemes sit at different levels and that one prepares students for the other. Teaching both levels at once from the start ignores the fact that syllable-level work is what makes phoneme-level work possible. Students would be asked to manipulate units they cannot yet hear as separate.

subject: Teaching Reading
stem: Ms. Nakamura's first-grade student, who is learning English, follows multistep directions and answers yes-or-no questions accurately but rarely speaks in complete sentences during group discussion. Which approach best supports the student's oral language development?
choices: Keeping the content demanding while lowering the response demand, using partner turns, sentence frames, and wait time before the student speaks to the whole group
Simplifying the content so that the student needs only short, familiar phrases to participate
Calling on the student regularly for full-sentence answers in front of the group to build the habit of speaking
Referring the student for a speech and language evaluation, because the gap between understanding and speaking indicates a disorder
correct_answer: Keeping the content demanding while lowering the response demand, using partner turns, sentence frames, and wait time before the student speaks to the whole group
explanation: The question requires an understanding of how receptive and expressive language develop. Receptive language normally runs ahead of expressive language, so a student can understand far more than they can yet produce. Lowering the risk of the response through a partner turn and a sentence frame keeps the thinking demanding while making the language manageable, which is what moves a student from understanding to producing.

distractor_explanations.Simplifying the content so that the stud: Mistakes watering down content for scaffolding, since easing the thinking also removes the practice with complex sentence structures the student most needs. Simplifying the content lowers the thinking along with the language, so the student gets less practice with the very structures that need developing. The aim is to keep ideas complex while supporting how they are expressed.
distractor_explanations.Calling on the student regularly for ful: Trusts repeated public calling-on to build speech, though performing without a language frame raises anxiety instead of supplying the missing pattern. Public pressure raises anxiety and offers no linguistic support for how to build the sentence. A student who lacks the pattern does not gain it by being asked to perform without it.
distractor_explanations.Referring the student for a speech and l: Pathologizes a normal receptive-expressive gap in a developing language learner, reaching for a referral before documented instruction has had its chance. A receptive-expressive gap is typical of developing language learners, including students learning English, and does not by itself indicate a disorder. A referral should follow documented, well-supported instruction, not replace it.

subject: Teaching Reading
stem: Ms. Ochoa is writing a small-group lesson whose objective is phoneme substitution. She sketches four possible tasks. Which example best supports that objective?
choices: Students sort picture cards by whether the name of the picture begins with /m/
Students say mat, are told to change /m/ to /s/, and say the new word
Students blend the sounds /s/ /a/ /t/ to say sat
Students clap the three syllables in Saturday
correct_answer: Students say mat, are told to change /m/ to /s/, and say the new word
explanation: The question requires an understanding of how to evaluate an example against a specific instructional goal. Substitution is a manipulation task: the student holds the word in memory, removes one phoneme, inserts another, and produces the result. Turning mat into sat does exactly that, at the phoneme level and at the right level of difficulty for the stated objective.

distractor_explanations.Students sort picture cards by whether t: Treats isolating and sorting initial sounds as manipulation, when recognizing a phoneme is only the prerequisite for changing one and hearing what the change produces. Sorting by initial sound asks students to isolate and compare one phoneme across words. That is a beginning-level identification task; it does not require changing a word and hearing what the change produces.
distractor_explanations.Students blend the sounds /s/ /a/ /t/ to: Accepts blending as substitution, though blending only combines sounds while substitution also requires holding the word in memory, removing one, and inserting another. Blending asks students to combine sounds into a word. It is a prerequisite for substitution rather than the same operation, because nothing is removed or replaced.
distractor_explanations.Students clap the three syllables in Sat: Overlooks that syllables are far larger units than phonemes, so a clapping task never reaches the level the objective names. Clapping the syllables in Saturday works at the syllable level, far above the individual phoneme, and the operation is segmentation rather than substitution.

subject: Teaching Reading
stem: Ms. Ferrand needs to screen the phonemic awareness of a kindergarten student who recently enrolled and whose strongest language is not English. Which approach is most appropriate?
choices: Administering the English task and treating a low score as evidence of a phonological deficit
Skipping phonemic awareness and screening letter knowledge instead, because letter names are language-neutral
Using oral phonemic awareness tasks in the student's strongest language where possible, because awareness of sound structure transfers across languages
Delaying screening until the student has enough English to complete the task in English
correct_answer: Using oral phonemic awareness tasks in the student's strongest language where possible, because awareness of sound structure transfers across languages
explanation: The question requires an understanding of how assessment can respond to students' varied language experience. Phonemic awareness is a metalinguistic insight into how speech is structured, and once acquired it transfers across languages. Screening in the student's stronger language therefore reveals what the student actually knows instead of measuring how much English they have learned.

distractor_explanations.Administering the English task and treat: Reads a language difference as a deficit, drawing conclusions about phonemic awareness from a task that mostly measures knowledge of English sounds. A task that requires manipulating English sounds a student has barely heard measures English sound knowledge, not the underlying capacity. Treating the result as a deficit risks mistaking a language difference for a disability.
distractor_explanations.Skipping phonemic awareness and screenin: Swaps in letter knowledge as a proxy, though naming letters and segmenting spoken sounds are different constructs and one cannot stand in for the other. Letter knowledge is a useful early measure, but it assesses a different construct. A student can name many letters and still be unable to segment the sounds in a spoken word, so it cannot stand in for a phonemic awareness screen.
distractor_explanations.Delaying screening until the student has: Ties assessment to English proficiency, delaying instruction on the assumption that a student must master the language before anything can be measured or taught. Waiting for English proficiency stalls instruction. The purpose of screening is to decide what to teach now, and a student's development can be assessed and supported without waiting for English to catch up.

subject: Teaching Reading
stem: Mr. Duffy teaches one letter a week in alphabetical order. Students who already know letter names learn letters such as b and m easily but struggle with h and w. Which revision is best supported by what is known about the alphabetic principle?
choices: Dropping letter names from instruction and teaching only sounds, since names distract students from the alphabetic principle
Teaching only the letters whose names contain their sounds first and delaying the remaining letters until second grade
Keeping the alphabetical order but spending more weeks on each letter so that students have additional time to learn it
Teaching the letter name and sound together, pointing out where the name contains the sound, and scheduling extra distributed practice for letters such as h and w where it does not
correct_answer: Teaching the letter name and sound together, pointing out where the name contains the sound, and scheduling extra distributed practice for letters such as h and w where it does not
explanation: The question requires an understanding of how letter-name knowledge supports the alphabetic principle. For many letters the name contains the sound, so the name acts as a built-in retrieval cue. For letters such as h and w the name offers no cue at all, so those letters need explicit statement of the sound plus additional, spaced practice. Teaching names and sounds together exploits the cue where it exists and compensates where it does not.

distractor_explanations.Dropping letter names from instruction a: Sets letter names against letter sounds and discards a built-in retrieval cue that helps students learn the sound for most letters. Letter names are an asset rather than a distraction. For most letters the name contains the sound, and children who know names generally learn the corresponding sounds more readily than those who do not.
distractor_explanations.Teaching only the letters whose names co: Treats difficulty as a reason for delay, leaving holes in the set of mappings students need and shrinking the words they can decode. Delaying the harder letters until second grade leaves gaps in the very set of mappings students need for decoding. Difficulty is a reason for more practice and better support, not for postponement.
distractor_explanations.Keeping the alphabetical order but spend: Adds time instead of changing method, missing that the obstacle is an absent name-to-sound cue that calls for explicit teaching and spaced practice. More time per letter does not address the source of the difficulty, which is the absence of a name-to-sound cue. Alphabetical order also ignores the advantage of teaching letters that unlock many words early.

subject: Teaching Reading
stem: Ms. Barr's kindergarten sound wall displays the English phonemes with their common spellings and mouth pictures. Several of her students speak Spanish at home. Which adaptation would best use the display to support those students' phonemic awareness?
choices: Marking the phonemes that do not occur in Spanish and building in frequent targeted practice on those, while keeping the wall as a shared reference for the whole class
Removing the English phonemes that do not occur in Spanish so that the display matches the students' current sound system
Expecting the students to acquire the new English phonemes through daily read-alouds, since exposure builds awareness
Using the sound wall only with the English-speaking students and giving the Spanish-speaking students picture cards instead
correct_answer: Marking the phonemes that do not occur in Spanish and building in frequent targeted practice on those, while keeping the wall as a shared reference for the whole class
explanation: The question requires an understanding of how classroom displays can be adapted for students with different language experience. Marking which phonemes are new turns the wall from a poster into an instructional plan: the teacher knows which mouth pictures to revisit and which contrasts need extra listening practice. Keeping it shared serves everyone and holds the same expectations for all students.

distractor_explanations.Removing the English phonemes that do no: Confuses matching the display to students' current sound system with adapting it, cutting out the very contrasts they most need to learn. Removing the difficult phonemes removes exactly what these students most need to learn. A display should organize instruction around the contrasts students have not yet acquired, not around the ones they already have.
distractor_explanations.Expecting the students to acquire the ne: Expects immersion to do the work unaided, though a phoneme a student cannot yet hear must be noticed, named, and practiced. Incidental exposure in read-alouds is not enough for phonemes a student does not yet perceive. New contrasts have to be noticed, named, and practiced before they are available for reading and spelling.
distractor_explanations.Using the sound wall only with the Engli: Reads differentiation as handing some students lesser materials, when it should change how a shared resource is used and how much practice it receives. Separate materials signal lower expectations and remove access to core instruction. The same wall, used deliberately and with additional practice, supports every student in the room.

subject: Teaching Reading
stem: Ms. Vega's students readily produce rhymes and blend onsets and rimes, but after several weeks most still cannot segment a three-phoneme word such as ship into its separate sounds. Which interpretation is most accurate?
choices: Rhyming is unrelated to reading development, so the time spent on it was wasted
Rhyme and onset-rime awareness are precursors that do not automatically produce phoneme-level awareness, so instruction should add explicit segmentation work at the phoneme level
The students likely have a phonological processing disorder and should be referred for evaluation
Continued rhyming practice will eventually produce phoneme awareness on its own
correct_answer: Rhyme and onset-rime awareness are precursors that do not automatically produce phoneme-level awareness, so instruction should add explicit segmentation work at the phoneme level
explanation: The question requires an understanding of how phonological awareness develops into phonemic awareness. Rhyme and onset-rime work builds the habit of attending to the sound structure of words, but holding three separate phonemes in sequence is a harder demand that requires its own instruction. The accurate reading of these data is that the students are ready for the next level, not that the earlier instruction failed.

distractor_explanations.Rhyming is unrelated to reading developm: Dismisses rhyme work as wasted effort because it proved insufficient, overlooking that it lays the foundation the next step builds on. Rhyme and onset-rime awareness are well-established contributors to later reading and belong in a systematic sequence. Dropping them would remove the foundation that the next step builds on.
distractor_explanations.The students likely have a phonological: Blames stalled progress on a student deficit and skips the required step of first delivering explicit instruction at the level where students are struggling. Several weeks without progress at the phoneme level is a signal to change instruction, not evidence of a disorder.
