A referral is premature before students have received explicit, systematic teaching at the level where they are struggling.
distractor_explanations.Continued rhyming practice will eventual: Expects awareness at the larger-unit level to trickle down on its own, when reaching phonemes requires explicit teaching to bridge the levels. Larger-unit awareness does not automatically generalize to smaller units. Students can rhyme fluently and still be unable to count or isolate the individual phonemes in a word.

subject: Teaching Reading
stem: A kindergarten teacher wants to build students' expressive language during a unit on plants. Which routine would best accomplish this goal?
choices: Giving students a page of plant words to trace and copy
Asking students to listen quietly while the teacher reads a book about how seeds travel
Having partners take turns telling how their own seedling changed, using the frame "First ___, then ___, and now ___"
Showing students labeled photos of roots, stems, and leaves and asking them to point to the stem
correct_answer: Having partners take turns telling how their own seedling changed, using the frame "First ___, then ___, and now ___"
explanation: The question requires an understanding of how expressive language is developed. Expressive language grows only when students produce extended oral output themselves. The sentence frame lowers the planning load so students can spend their effort on putting a real observation into words, and the partner format guarantees every student a turn instead of only the volunteers who already speak readily.

distractor_explanations.Giving students a page of plant words to: Assuming that tracing and copying words builds spoken language Option (D) is incorrect. Tracing and copying are print and handwriting tasks. They produce marks on a page rather than spoken language, so they leave the expressive channel unexercised.
distractor_explanations.Asking students to listen quietly while: Equating rich receptive input with the development of expressive output Option (A) is incorrect. A read-aloud supplies rich vocabulary and sentence structures, but it asks students to receive language, not to generate it. Rich input is a necessary companion to expressive work, not a substitute for it.
distractor_explanations.Showing students labeled photos of roots: Treating pointing and recognition responses as if they forced students to generate language Option (C) is incorrect. Pointing to a named part requires students to map a word they hear onto a picture, which taps receptive vocabulary. The student produces no sentence and no idea of their own.

subject: Teaching Reading
stem: A first-grade teacher is planning the order in which phonemic awareness skills will be taught across the year. Which sequence moves from less complex to more complex?
choices: Deleting a phoneme from a word → substituting a phoneme → blending individual phonemes → recognizing rhymes
Blending individual phonemes → recognizing rhymes → blending onset and rime → deleting a phoneme from a word
Recognizing rhymes → deleting a phoneme from a word → substituting a phoneme → blending onset and rime
Recognizing rhymes → blending onset and rime → blending individual phonemes → deleting a phoneme from a word
correct_answer: Recognizing rhymes → blending onset and rime → blending individual phonemes → deleting a phoneme from a word
explanation: The question requires an understanding of the developmental progression within phonemic awareness. Larger sound units are easier to perceive than smaller ones. Working with whole words through rhyme comes first, then splitting words into the two chunks of onset and rime, then attending to each separate phoneme, and finally manipulating phonemes by deleting or substituting them, which adds a memory load because the student must hold the word in mind while changing it.

distractor_explanations.Deleting a phoneme from a word → substit: Presenting the developmental progression in reverse, as though mastering the hardest operation first would carry the easier ones along Option (B) is incorrect. This is the progression run backwards. Deletion and substitution depend on the student already being able to hear and hold individual phonemes, so starting there asks for the hardest operation before its prerequisites exist.
distractor_explanations.Blending individual phonemes → recognizi: Placing analysis of individual phonemes ahead of word-level rhyme work Option (C) is incorrect. Individual phoneme blending is placed first, before rhyme, and onset-rime work is pushed to third. Phoneme-level work is more demanding than word-level rhyme work, so this order asks students to analyze the smallest units before they have practiced hearing the largest ones.
distractor_explanations.Recognizing rhymes → deleting a phoneme: Assuming deletion and substitution can be taught before students isolate individual phonemes Option (D) is incorrect. This order jumps from rhyme straight to deletion and substitution and leaves individual phoneme blending and segmenting for last, even though manipulation cannot succeed until students can isolate the separate sounds in a word.

subject: Teaching Reading
stem: A kindergarten teacher wants a quick, informal check of whether students can segment a word into its individual phonemes. Which task best provides that information?
choices: Asking students to clap once for each part they hear in the word table
Asking students to push a counter forward for each sound they hear in the word dog
Asking students to pick the picture that rhymes with dog from two choices
Asking students to point to the letter that begins the word dog on an alphabet chart
correct_answer: Asking students to push a counter forward for each sound they hear in the word dog
explanation: The question requires an understanding of how an informal assessment isolates one specific skill. Moving one counter per sound in a three-phoneme word requires the student to isolate each phoneme in order, and the number of counters a child produces shows immediately whether that child is working at the phoneme level or is still responding to larger units.

distractor_explanations.Asking students to clap once for each pa: Treating syllable tapping as evidence of phoneme-level segmentation Option (A) is incorrect. Clapping the parts of table measures syllable awareness. A child can clap two beats perfectly while hearing no individual phonemes at all, so this task cannot answer the question the teacher is asking.
distractor_explanations.Asking students to pick the picture that: Accepting rhyme judgment as proof that a student can analyze a word's internal sound sequence Option (C) is incorrect. Rhyme judgment works at the level of whole words and their endings. It requires no analysis of the internal sound sequence and therefore reveals nothing about segmentation.
distractor_explanations.Asking students to point to the letter t: Using a print-based letter-identification task to measure an oral listening skill Option (D) is incorrect. Pointing to a letter on an alphabet chart measures letter knowledge, which involves print. Phonemic awareness is an oral skill assessed without any print at all.

subject: Teaching Reading
stem: During a shared reading of a big book, a kindergarten student points to the illustration instead of the print and begins at the bottom of the page. Which concept of print should the teacher address first?
choices: That print, not pictures, carries the message, and that English print is read top to bottom and left to right
That an uppercase letter marks the beginning of a sentence
That a book has a title page that names it
That spaces mark the boundaries between words
correct_answer: That print, not pictures, carries the message, and that English print is read top to bottom and left to right
explanation: The question requires an understanding of the order in which concepts of print develop. Before a child can track print, the child has to know two things: that the print is what carries the story, and that it travels in a fixed direction. Pointing to pictures and starting at the bottom shows both are missing, so they are addressed first; capitalization, book parts, and word boundaries are taught once the child can follow a line of print.

distractor_explanations.That an uppercase letter marks the begin: Teaching capitalization rules before establishing that print carries meaning and travels in a fixed direction Option (B) is incorrect. Capitalization at sentence openings is a real concept of print, but it is meaningful only to a student who has already located the print and is following it. Teaching it first leaves the underlying tracking problem untouched.
distractor_explanations.That a book has a title page that names: Treating book-handling knowledge as the remedy for a difficulty with print directionality Option (C) is incorrect. Identifying the title page is book-handling knowledge. It tells a child how a book is organized, not where to begin on a page or which way the print moves.
distractor_explanations.That spaces mark the boundaries between: Introducing word-boundary awareness before a student can locate and follow a line of print Option (D) is incorrect. Word boundaries matter for matching spoken words to printed words while tracking, but a child who is not yet starting at the top of the page has no line of print to apply them to.

subject: Teaching Reading
stem: A kindergarten student can tell the teacher that the spoken word sun has three sounds and can blend /s/ /u/ /n/ back into the word. Shown the printed word sun, the student cannot read it. This performance most strongly indicates that the student has not yet developed
choices: knowledge of the names of the letters
the ability to hear individual phonemes in spoken words
an understanding that letters stand for the sounds in spoken words
awareness that print is read from left to right
correct_answer: an understanding that letters stand for the sounds in spoken words
explanation: The question requires an understanding of the alphabetic principle. The student's oral performance shows that phonemic awareness is already in place, so the missing piece is the insight that the letters on the page are a code for those sounds. Without that mapping, a printed word carries no retrievable sound values, and instruction must make the letter-to-sound correspondence visible and explicit.

distractor_explanations.knowledge of the names of the letters: Treating letter-name knowledge as the mechanism that makes reading possible Option (D) is incorrect. Letter names help a student remember letter sounds, but reciting names is neither necessary nor sufficient for reading. A child can know every letter name and still not grasp that the letters represent the sounds in a word.
distractor_explanations.the ability to hear individual phonemes: Attributing a failure to read printed words to a phonemic awareness deficit Option (A) is incorrect. The student segmented and blended the sounds of sun orally, which is direct evidence that the phonemes are perceptible to this child. Adding more phonemic awareness practice would reteach a skill the student has already demonstrated.
distractor_explanations.awareness that print is read from left t: Explaining a breakdown in letter-sound mapping as a problem with print directionality Option (C) is incorrect. A directionality problem produces tracking errors, such as reading the right-hand page first or sweeping to the wrong margin. This student is not mis-tracking; the student is not recovering sounds from letters at all.

subject: Teaching Reading
stem: A first-grade teacher is setting up the literacy environment. Which use of classroom materials would best support students' phonemic awareness?
choices: An alphabet frieze with one keyword picture for each letter
A bulletin board displaying student writing samples with illustrations
A word wall of high-frequency words arranged in alphabetical order
A sound wall that groups pictures by how each phoneme is produced in the mouth
correct_answer: A sound wall that groups pictures by how each phoneme is produced in the mouth
explanation: The question requires an understanding of how classroom materials can make the sound structure of language visible. A sound wall organized by articulation directs attention to the phonemes themselves, to how the mouth forms them and how one differs from its neighbors. That keeps the work at the oral, speech level that phonemic awareness occupies instead of skipping ahead to print.

distractor_explanations.An alphabet frieze with one keyword pict: Equating a one-picture-per-letter alphabet frieze with instruction in phonemic awareness Option (C) is incorrect. A one-picture-per-letter alphabet frieze supports beginning letter-sound correspondence, which is useful but different. Because it shows twenty-six letters, it also risks leaving students with the impression that English has only twenty-six sounds.
distractor_explanations.A bulletin board displaying student writ: Assuming that displaying student work on a wall supports work on the sound structure of language Option (D) is incorrect. Displaying finished writing builds a print-rich room and values students' composition work, but the display itself gives no opportunity to hear, isolate, or manipulate sounds.
distractor_explanations.A word wall of high-frequency words arra: Mistaking an alphabetically sorted word wall for a tool that trains phoneme manipulation Option (A) is incorrect. An alphabetically arranged word wall sorts words by letter name and helps students locate and spell known words. It supports sight-word reading and writing, not the ability to hear and manipulate individual sounds.

subject: Teaching Reading
stem: Ms. Alvarez is preparing an onset-rime lesson for her kindergarten class. Several students are English learners who are still building oral vocabulary in English. Which modification to the lesson materials would best support those students?
choices: Removing the pictures and working with spoken words only, so that students attend to sounds rather than images
Pairing each spoken word with a picture whose name is already familiar, so students can manipulate the sounds of a word they know
Replacing the spoken words with printed word cards so students can see the shared rime
Adding a written sorting worksheet for students to complete on their own after the lesson
correct_answer: Pairing each spoken word with a picture whose name is already familiar, so students can manipulate the sounds of a word they know
explanation: The question requires an understanding of how to modify examples and materials for particular learners. Onset-rime work is an oral task, and these students may not yet have a stable label for the word being taken apart. Pictures with familiar referents carry the vocabulary load, so the students' attention stays on the sound structure instead of on guessing what the word means.

distractor_explanations.Removing the pictures and working with s: Removing visual vocabulary supports on the assumption that images distract from auditory processing Option (A) is incorrect. Taking pictures away raises the language demand precisely for the students who need it lowered. A child who is unsure what the word means cannot manipulate its parts, so the task would end up measuring vocabulary rather than phonological awareness.
distractor_explanations.Replacing the spoken words with printed: Converting an oral phonological task into a print-based decoding task Option (C) is incorrect. Putting the words in print shifts the task toward orthography and decoding. Onset-rime manipulation is meant to be done with the ear, and requiring print adds a demand these students are not ready for.
distractor_explanations.Adding a written sorting worksheet for s: Substituting an independent written worksheet for oral modeling and guided practice Option (D) is incorrect. An independent written sort removes both the oral response and the teacher's modeling, so students lose the feedback that tells them whether they split the word in the right place.

subject: Teaching Reading
stem: During a phoneme segmentation activity, a kindergarten student correctly segments the familiar two-syllable words rabbit, pencil, and wagon but cannot segment the less familiar two-syllable words compass, falcon, and beacon. Which interpretation of this pattern best guides the teacher's next step?
choices: The student's difficulty is limited to words of two syllables, so the teacher should keep phonemic awareness tasks to single-syllable words
The student cannot yet isolate individual phonemes, so the teacher should restart segmentation instruction with shorter, one-syllable words
The student knows the second set of words too poorly in speech to hold them in mind while manipulating sounds, so the teacher should build oral familiarity with those words first
The student has not learned the letter-sound correspondences in the second set of words, so the teacher should teach those letters before returning to segmentation
correct_answer: The student knows the second set of words too poorly in speech to hold them in mind while manipulating sounds, so the teacher should build oral familiarity with those words first
explanation: The question requires an understanding of how oral language supports phonemic awareness. Phonemic awareness tasks are performed on spoken words, so a student must already know a word well enough to hold it in memory and then reflect on its sound structure. Because this student segments two-syllable words accurately whenever the words are familiar, the ability to isolate phonemes is present; what breaks down is the student's spoken knowledge of the less familiar words. The teacher's next step is to build that oral vocabulary through talk, pictures, and repeated spoken use before asking the student to take those words apart again.

distractor_explanations.The student's difficulty is limited to w: Attributing the failures to word length when both sets of words contained the same number of syllables Option (D) is incorrect. Both sets of words have two syllables, so syllable count cannot account for the split between the words the student segmented and the words the student could not. Restricting tasks to single-syllable words would narrow the activity without addressing the vocabulary gap behind the failures.
distractor_explanations.The student cannot yet isolate individua: Treating failure on a segmentation task as proof that phonemic awareness itself is missing, without first asking whether the words used were known to the student Option (A) is incorrect. The student already segments familiar two-syllable words accurately, which is direct evidence that the ability to isolate phonemes has developed. Restarting with one-syllable words would reteach a skill the student has demonstrated while leaving the real obstacle, unfamiliar vocabulary, untouched.
distractor_explanations.The student has not learned the letter-s: Confusing phonemic awareness, an oral task done without print, with phonics instruction that depends on letter-sound correspondences Option (C) is incorrect. Segmentation is an oral task done with no print in view, so letter knowledge is not required to perform it. Letter-sound correspondences belong to phonics and decoding, and they cannot explain why the student succeeds on one set of spoken words and fails on the other.

subject: Teaching Reading
stem: A first-grade teacher says, "Say bend. Now say bend again without the /b/." A student responds "ben." This response most strongly indicates a difficulty with
choices: blending separate phonemes into a whole word
recognizing that two spoken words share the same rime
hearing the final sound in a spoken word
locating the position of a target phoneme within the sequence of sounds in a word
correct_answer: locating the position of a target phoneme within the sequence of sounds in a word
explanation: The question requires an understanding of what phoneme deletion tasks reveal about a student. The student carried out the mechanics of the operation but took off the wrong phoneme, removing the final sound instead of the initial one. That pattern points to the positional analysis of the word, knowing which slot in the sound sequence the target occupies, rather than to any inability to perform the deletion itself.

distractor_explanations.blending separate phonemes into a whole: Confusing phoneme deletion with the opposite operation of blending sounds into a word Option (C) is incorrect. Blending runs in the opposite direction, assembling separate sounds into a word, and nothing in this response shows a blending failure. The student produced a well-formed word.
distractor_explanations.recognizing that two spoken words share: Explaining an error in phoneme manipulation by appealing to word-level rhyme awareness Option (D) is incorrect. Rime recognition compares the endings of whole words and is a much earlier-developing skill. It cannot explain an error made while manipulating a single phoneme inside one word.
distractor_explanations.hearing the final sound in a spoken word: Interpreting removal of the wrong phoneme as an inability to perceive the final sound Option (A) is incorrect. The student clearly perceived the final sound; dropping it requires attending to it. The error is not that the final sound went unheard but that the student searched the word in the wrong place.

subject: Teaching Reading
stem: A preschool teacher points to the cover of a book and says, "This tells us the name of our book." Which concept of print is the teacher introducing?
choices: That a book is made of parts with distinct functions, and that the cover announces what the book is about
That print moves from left to right across the page
That each spoken word is matched by a printed word
That a lowercase letter can be matched to its uppercase form
correct_answer: That a book is made of parts with distinct functions, and that the cover announces what the book is about
explanation: The question requires an understanding of how book-handling knowledge is taught. Naming the cover and explaining what it does builds the idea that a book is organized into parts, each with its own job. That idea is what later lets students use the table of contents, headings, and page numbers as tools for finding information.

distractor_explanations.That print moves from left to right acro: Treating an explanation of book parts as instruction in print directionality Option (B) is incorrect. Directionality is built by tracking print line by line during shared reading, not by talking about the cover. The two ideas live at different levels: one is about the page, the other is about the book as an object.
distractor_explanations.That each spoken word is matched by a pr: Confusing word awareness, the matching of speech to print, with knowledge of how books are built Option (C) is incorrect. Matching spoken words to printed words is word awareness, a concept demonstrated by pointing under each word as a line is read. The cover comment does not involve matching speech to print.
distractor_explanations.That a lowercase letter can be matched t: Mistaking letter-form matching for an understanding of book structure Option (D) is incorrect. Matching uppercase and lowercase forms is letter-level knowledge, far more fine-grained than what the teacher is pointing at. A child can be taught letter forms without any understanding of how a book is put together.

subject: Teaching Reading
stem: Which activity most directly demonstrates the alphabetic principle to beginning readers?
choices: Students push a letter tile into each box of a three-box chart as they say the sounds in mop, then run a finger under the tiles to blend them into the word
Students clap once for each part they hear in rabbit, then sort picture cards by how many parts the names have
Students sort picture cards by whether the names begin with the same sound
Students reread a familiar predictable text to a partner to build expression
correct_answer: Students push a letter tile into each box of a three-box chart as they say the sounds in mop, then run a finger under the tiles to blend them into the word
explanation: The question requires an understanding of how the alphabetic principle is made visible to novices. Placing one letter tile per spoken sound attaches a written symbol to each phoneme the student can already hear, and sweeping a finger under the tiles to blend them shows that reading a word means recovering the sounds its letters stand for. The oral skill the student already has is thereby connected to print.

distractor_explanations.Students clap once for each part they he: Treating syllable-level phonological work as instruction in the alphabetic principle Option (B) is incorrect. Clapping and counting syllables operates entirely in speech with no letters present. It is phonological awareness at the syllable level, which sits below the alphabetic principle.
distractor_explanations.Students sort picture cards by whether t: Mistaking a print-free phonemic awareness sort for work on letter-sound correspondence Option (C) is incorrect. Sorting pictures by initial sound is phonemic awareness, and it is deliberately done without print. Because no letters appear, nothing about the letter-to-sound relationship can be demonstrated.
distractor_explanations.Students reread a familiar predictable t: Assuming that fluency practice with familiar text builds understanding of the alphabetic principle Option (D) is incorrect. Partner rereading builds automaticity and prosody on text the student already knows. It asks for whole-word recognition and expression rather than for analysis of individual letter-sound correspondences.

subject: Teaching Reading
stem: Which activity primarily develops students' awareness of syllables in spoken words?
choices: Asking students to change the /k/ in cat to /h/ and say the new word
Asking students to clap once for each part they hear in the word elephant
Asking students to say which word in a set of three does not rhyme with cat
Asking students to name the first sound they hear in cat
correct_answer: Asking students to clap once for each part they hear in the word elephant
explanation: The question requires an understanding of the levels within phonological awareness. Syllables are the largest units below the whole word, and clapping one beat per part lets students feel the internal shape of a long word without requiring them to notice individual phonemes, which is a later and more demanding step.

distractor_explanations.Asking students to change the /k/ in cat: Treating phoneme substitution, the most advanced level, as a syllable-level task Option (D) is incorrect. Substitution requires manipulating individual phonemes while holding the rest of the word in memory, which is the most advanced level of phonemic awareness and far beyond syllable work.
distractor_explanations.Asking students to say which word in a s: Mistaking a rhyme oddity task for work on the internal structure of a single word Option (B) is incorrect. An odd-one-out rhyme task compares the endings of whole words. Attention goes to the rime shared by two of the words, not to how any single word is divided internally.
distractor_explanations.Asking students to name the first sound: Confusing isolation of a single phoneme with awareness of syllables Option (C) is incorrect. Isolating the first sound is phoneme-level work, a finer grain than the syllable. A student who can do this has already moved past syllable awareness.

subject: Teaching Reading
stem: A fourth-grade teacher notices that several students struggle to follow multi-step oral directions during science investigations. Which practice would best strengthen these students' receptive language?
choices: Asking students to write a summary of the investigation once they have finished
Making the teacher's explanations longer and more complex so that students build stamina
Asking students to listen to the directions and then tell a partner what they will do first, second, and third
Providing the directions in writing only, so students can reread them as they work
correct_answer: Asking students to listen to the directions and then tell a partner what they will do first, second, and third
explanation: The question requires an understanding of how receptive language is strengthened. Listening is not passive absorption; asking students to hold a sequence in mind and then restate it in order forces active processing of what was heard. It also gives the teacher immediate evidence of where the sequence broke down, which is exactly what a written alternative cannot do.

distractor_explanations.Asking students to write a summary of th: Treating written summary produced after the fact as training in receptive language Option (C) is incorrect. Writing a summary afterward is an expressive task that asks students to produce language about meaning. It comes after comprehension has already happened and does not exercise the decoding of spoken input.
distractor_explanations.Making the teacher's explanations longer: Assuming that increasing the difficulty of oral input builds listening capacity Option (D) is incorrect. Longer and denser input overloads working memory for students who are already losing the sequence. Difficulty without support produces failure rather than growth.
distractor_explanations.Providing the directions in writing only: Routing the task through print so that the listening skill needing practice is bypassed Option (B) is incorrect. Written directions route the task through reading and remove the listening practice these students need. Accommodating around a weak skill is different from developing it.

subject: Teaching Reading
stem: Why is oral phonemic segmentation considered a prerequisite for profiting from instruction in the alphabetic principle?
choices: Because students must know the names of the letters before they can learn the sounds of the letters
Because segmentation practice is what makes oral reading fluent
Because students cannot hear rhyme until they can segment words into phonemes
Because students must be able to hear the separate sounds in a word before a letter can be understood as standing for one of those sounds
correct_answer: Because students must be able to hear the separate sounds in a word before a letter can be understood as standing for one of those sounds
explanation: The question requires an understanding of the relationship between phonemic awareness and the alphabetic principle. The alphabetic principle holds that letters map onto phonemes. For a child who does not yet perceive the separate sounds inside a spoken word, there is nothing for the letter to attach to; segmentation supplies the units that the letters then represent.

distractor_explanations.Because students must know the names of: Treating letter-name knowledge as the prerequisite for grasping the alphabetic principle Option (B) is incorrect. Letter names are convenient mnemonics for remembering sounds, but they are a separate strand of learning. The essential prerequisite is auditory, not the ability to recite the alphabet.
distractor_explanations.Because segmentation practice is what ma: Assigning phonemic segmentation the later role of producing fluent oral reading Option (C) is incorrect. Fluency develops through repeated reading of connected text and grows after decoding is underway. Segmentation supports the mapping of letters to sounds, which is a different contributor.
distractor_explanations.Because students cannot hear rhyme until: Reversing the developmental order so that rhyme is made to depend on phoneme segmentation Option (D) is incorrect. The order is reversed: children recognize rhyme before they can segment phonemes. Rhyme is word-level and appears earlier, so it cannot depend on a later-developing skill.

subject: Teaching Reading
stem: Which classroom practice makes the best use of a sound wall during daily phonics instruction?
choices: Having students produce the target phoneme and check their mouth position against the card before reading words that contain that sound
Having students copy every word on the sound wall into their notebooks each Monday
Using the sound wall as a display that students pass by during the day but never revisit
Having students put the sound cards back in alphabetical order at the end of each week
correct_answer: Having students produce the target phoneme and check their mouth position against the card before reading words that contain that sound
explanation: The question requires an understanding of how classroom materials become instructional tools. Referring students to the wall immediately before they read words with that sound ties the physical production of the phoneme to the letters they are about to decode, so the display does its work at the moment it can help instead of sitting behind the students as decoration.

distractor_explanations.Having students copy every word on the s: Turning an oral reference tool into a transcription exercise Option (B) is incorrect. Copying turns an oral reference tool into a transcription exercise. The time goes into forming letters, which draws attention away from hearing and saying the sound.
distractor_explanations.Using the sound wall as a display that s: Assuming that posting a display is equivalent to teaching with it Option (C) is incorrect. A display that is never referred to during teaching is wallpaper. Materials influence learning through repeated, purposeful use in lessons, not through their presence in the room.
distractor_explanations.Having students put the sound cards back: Imposing the spelling system's alphabetical order on a wall organized by sound Option (D) is incorrect. Alphabetical order is the logic of the spelling system. Imposing it on a wall built around sounds undoes the very organization that makes the wall useful and suggests again that letters and sounds pair one to one.
